summary: Blind model introspection: per-organ canonical-values audit, 2 independent rounds

A.organ: address (agent autonomy / authority relative to human supervisor)

values.name: Sheridan-Verplank 10 Levels of Automation (LOA)
values.reference: Sheridan & Verplank (1978), MIT; popularized in Sheridan, Telerobotics, Automation, and Human Supervisory Control (1992)
values.justification: The foundational ordinal scale (1 = human does everything ... 10 = computer acts autonomously, ignores human) that is THE canonical backbone for autonomy-vs-deference; nearly all later taxonomies cite it.

values.name: Levels 1-4: Computer offers no/some/narrowed/one decision option (human decides and acts)
values.reference: Sheridan & Verplank 10-level scale, lower band
values.justification: Defines the high-deference end: the agent only suggests; the human retains full decision and execution authority.

values.name: Level 5: Computer executes the suggestion if the human approves
values.reference: Sheridan & Verplank 10-level scale, level 5
values.justification: The canonical 'human-in-the-loop / approval gate' point — the agent proposes and acts only on explicit approval; this is the prototypical 'defer for approval' setting.

values.name: Levels 6-7: Computer allows the human a restricted veto window / acts then necessarily informs
values.reference: Sheridan & Verplank 10-level scale, levels 6-7
values.justification: The 'human-on-the-loop' band — the agent acts autonomously by default but the human can intervene; canonical for supervised autonomy.

values.name: Levels 8-10: Computer informs only if asked / only if it decides to / decides everything autonomously
values.reference: Sheridan & Verplank 10-level scale, upper band
values.justification: The full-autonomy end where the agent self-authorizes and human oversight is minimal or eliminated — the canonical 'acts on its own' extreme.

values.name: Stage-decomposed LOA (Acquisition / Analysis / Decision / Action)
values.reference: Parasuraman, Sheridan & Wickens (2000), 'A Model for Types and Levels of Human Interaction with Automation', IEEE SMC-A
values.justification: Refines the single scalar into a per-stage level, the standard modern correction showing autonomy is not one number; widely cited extension of the backbone.

values.name: Human-in-the-loop / on-the-loop / out-of-the-loop
values.reference: Common HCI / autonomous-systems and defense (DoD) terminology; 'out-of-the-loop performance problem', Endsley & Kiris (1995)
values.justification: The collapsed three-bucket vernacular that practitioners actually use; a recognized coarse projection of the LOA scale onto agent-supervision practice.

values.name: SAE J3016 Driving Automation Levels 0-5
values.reference: SAE International J3016 (2014, rev. 2021)
values.justification: A domain-specific but globally standardized closed enum of the same autonomy-vs-human-fallback dimension; canonical exemplar that the dimension admits formal standards.

A.evidenceNeeded: Confirmation of the intended granularity: whether "address" wants the full 10-level Sheridan-Verplank ordinal scale, the 4-stage Parasuraman model, or the coarse in/on/out-of-the-loop trichotomy. Also useful: whether the project treats autonomy as a single scalar or as per-action-type authority (which would favor the stage-decomposed or capability-scoped framings over the classic single LOA enum), and whether any LLM-agent-specific autonomy taxonomy (e.g., agentic 'tool-use approval' modes) should override the classic human-factors backbone.

values.name: Level 1 — Full manual / no automation (human does everything)
values.reference: Sheridan & Verplank (1978) 10-point LOA scale; Parasuraman, Sheridan & Wickens (2000)
values.justification: Canonical floor of the scale: the computer offers no assistance and the human makes and executes all decisions.

values.name: Level 2-3 — Decision support (computer suggests/narrows options)
values.reference: Sheridan & Verplank (1978), levels 2-3; Parasuraman et al. (2000)
values.justification: The system offers a complete set or a narrowed subset of decision alternatives, but the human chooses — classic 'advisory' autonomy band.

values.name: Level 4 — Recommend one action (human approves)
values.reference: Sheridan & Verplank (1978), level 4
values.justification: Computer suggests a single alternative; the human must still endorse it — the canonical 'recommend, await approval' tier.

values.name: Level 5 — Execute on human approval ('decide-then-do-if-approved')
values.reference: Sheridan & Verplank (1978), level 5
values.justification: System executes the suggestion only if the human assents; the explicit approval-gated action level central to this dimension.

values.name: Level 6 — Act unless vetoed within a window (delayed/revocable autonomy)
values.reference: Sheridan & Verplank (1978), level 6
values.justification: Computer acts after allowing the human a bounded time to veto — the 'management by exception' hinge between deferential and autonomous operation.

values.name: Level 7-8 — Act then inform (notify after execution)
values.reference: Sheridan & Verplank (1978), levels 7-8
values.justification: System acts autonomously and informs the human afterward (always, or only if asked) — autonomy with mandatory transparency.

values.name: Level 9-10 — Full autonomy (inform only if it decides to / ignore the human)
values.reference: Sheridan & Verplank (1978), levels 9-10
values.justification: Computer decides everything and acts autonomously, deciding itself whether to inform the human — the canonical ceiling of the scale.

B.evidenceNeeded: The Sheridan-Verplank 10-level LOA scale and the Parasuraman/Sheridan/Wickens (2000) Types-and-Levels model are the established canon for the 'how much autonomy / when to defer' dimension, so the classification as CLOSED is solid. Confidence would rise with confirmation of which granularity the project wants: the raw 10-level Sheridan scale, the 4-stage x level matrix of Parasuraman et al. (acquisition/analysis/decision/action each automatable separately), Endsley & Kaber's (1999) 10-level taxonomy, or a domain-specific collapse like SAE J3016 (L0-L5). The 10 levels are sometimes pragmatically binned into ~4-7 tiers (manual / advisory / approval-gated / veto-window / supervised-autonomous / full-autonomous); evidence on the intended resolution and whether the agent context treats autonomy as a single scalar vs. a per-function vector would sharpen the enumeration.

values.name: Self-critique / self-refinement (intrinsic self-feedback)
values.reference: Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023); Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023)
values.justification: Canonical agent appraisal mode where the same model generates natural-language feedback on its own output and iterates — no external signal required.

values.name: LLM-as-a-judge (model-graded evaluation)
values.reference: Zheng et al., MT-Bench/Chatbot Arena (2023); G-Eval (Liu et al., 2023)
values.justification: Established backbone for using a (possibly separate) LLM to score output against a rubric; now a standard acceptance mechanism in agent pipelines.

values.name: Verifier / discriminator model (learned outcome or process reward)
values.reference: Cobbe et al. GSM8K verifiers (2021); Lightman et al. 'Let's Verify Step by Step' (process reward models, 2023)
values.justification: A trained checker (outcome- or process-level) scores candidate solutions — a recognized, distinct appraisal strategy from self-critique.

values.name: Executable / test-oracle checking (ground-truth verification)
values.reference: Software testing test-oracle theory (Barr et al., 'The Oracle Problem in Software Testing', 2015); unit/property/regression tests
values.justification: Appraisal by running the artifact against a deterministic oracle (tests, compilers, type-checkers) — the strongest, field-standard acceptance criterion in SWE.

values.name: Acceptance criteria / specification conformance (validation against requirements)
values.reference: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 (requirements); IEEE 1012 Verification & Validation; Agile 'Definition of Done' / Gherkin acceptance criteria
values.justification: Checking output against an explicit, externally-defined spec or DoD is the canonical V&V distinction (verification vs. validation).

values.name: Human-in-the-loop review (external/operator appraisal)
values.reference: HCI human-automation literature (Parasuraman, Sheridan & Wickens, levels of automation, 2000)
values.justification: Deferring the accept/reject judgment to a human is a recognized point on the automation-of-decision spectrum and a real appraisal configuration.

values.name: No self-appraisal (open-loop / fire-and-forget)
values.reference: Control-theory open-loop vs. closed-loop control; baseline single-pass generation
values.justification: The degenerate but real end of the dimension — output declared done without any check — anchors the axis.

A.evidenceNeeded: A single authoritative survey that explicitly enumerates agent self-evaluation/acceptance strategies as a closed taxonomy (rather than my synthesis across SWE V&V, LLM-judge, and self-refinement literatures). A recognized cross-cutting framework — e.g., a 'verification strategy' taxonomy in an agent-architecture survey, or mapping these modes onto appraisal-theory dimensions from cognitive science — would confirm whether this is a true closed backbone or remains an open synthesis. Confirming whether 'verifier model', 'LLM-as-judge', and 'test-oracle' are treated as mutually exclusive categories vs. overlapping would sharpen the enumeration.

values.name: Intrinsic self-critique / self-refinement
values.reference: Self-Refine (Madaan et al. 2023); Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023); Constitutional AI self-critique (Bai et al. 2022)
values.justification: The agent appraises its own output with no external signal, generating feedback and revising — the canonical 'self-evaluation' mechanism in the LLM-agent literature.

values.name: External verifier / reward model
values.reference: Cobbe et al. 2021 (GSM8K training verifiers); RLHF reward models; LLM-as-a-judge (Zheng et al. 2023, MT-Bench)
values.justification: A separate model/critic scores candidate outputs — a distinct, widely-cited appraisal family where the evaluator is not the generator.

values.name: Executable test / oracle (verification against spec)
values.reference: V&V (IEEE 1012); Test-Driven Development (Beck); 'definition of done' (Scrum); the test oracle problem
values.justification: Acceptance is decided by running tests / checking a spec — the dominant software-engineering form of 'is it done?' and the most objective appraisal.

values.name: Sampling consensus / self-consistency
values.reference: Self-Consistency (Wang et al. 2022); majority-vote / ensemble decoding
values.justification: Multiple samples are drawn and agreement is used as the acceptance signal — a recognized statistical appraisal distinct from single-pass critique.

values.name: Ground-truth / validation comparison
values.reference: Verification-vs-Validation distinction (IEEE 1012, Boehm); supervised eval against gold labels
values.justification: Output is compared to a known-correct reference or real-world outcome — validation ('did we build the right thing') as opposed to internal verification.

values.name: Metacognitive confidence / calibration gate
values.reference: Metamemory monitoring & control (Nelson & Narens 1990); confidence calibration (Guo et al. 2017); TOTE test phase (Miller, Galanter & Pribram 1960)
values.justification: Acceptance gated on a self-reported/calibrated confidence threshold — the cognitive-science backbone for self-monitoring before terminating action.

B.evidenceNeeded: A survey paper that explicitly enumerates self-evaluation/verification strategies for LLM agents as a named taxonomy (e.g., a 'self-correction' or 'verification methods' survey) would confirm whether the field treats these as a closed backbone or merely a loose family. Also a controlled-vocabulary standard (analogous to IEEE 1012's V&V split) that fixes the member set would push this toward 'closed'; absence of any such canonical enum keeps it 'hybrid'.

values.name: Helpful, Honest, Harmless (HHH)
values.reference: Askell et al., "A General Language Assistant as a Laboratory for Alignment" (Anthropic, 2021)
values.justification: The field-standard triad framing the core value-constraints an aligned assistant must satisfy; the most widely cited canonical backbone for assistant guardrails.

values.name: Constitutional principles
values.reference: Bai et al., "Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback" (Anthropic, 2022)
values.justification: Establishes the explicit 'charter as a written constitution' pattern—a finite list of natural-language principles the model self-critiques against; the dimension's namesake construct.

values.name: Three Laws of Robotics
values.reference: Asimov, I, Robot (1942/1950)
values.justification: The archetypal precedence-ordered inviolable-constraint set; canonical reference for hard-priority safety hierarchies in agent design despite being fictional.

values.name: Usage / acceptable-use policy categories (harm taxonomy)
values.reference: OpenAI Usage Policies; Anthropic Usage Policy; ML Commons AI Safety / MLCommons hazard taxonomy
values.justification: The de-facto enumerated content-harm categories (CSAM, weapons/CBRN, violence, self-harm, privacy, illegal activity, hate) that operationalize 'do not' constraints across the industry.

values.name: Ethics principles (fairness, accountability, transparency, non-maleficence, autonomy)
values.reference: OECD AI Principles (2019); EU Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI (HLEG, 2019); Floridi & Cowls (2019)
values.justification: The recognized normative backbone for AI value-constraints, distilling bioethics principlism (Beauchamp & Childress) into AI; appears across governance frameworks.

values.name: NIST AI RMF trustworthiness characteristics
values.reference: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 (2023)
values.justification: A standards-body enumeration (valid/reliable, safe, secure/resilient, accountable/transparent, explainable, privacy-enhanced, fair) treated as the constraint set an agent is designed to uphold.

A.evidenceNeeded: Whether the field treats 'charter' as a closed enum versus an authoring slot is the crux. Confidence would rise with: (a) a survey paper consolidating agent-guardrail/constitution taxonomies to confirm no single closed enum dominates; (b) evidence of how widely the HHH triad vs. policy-harm-category lists are reused verbatim as canonical members vs. each deployment authoring its own principles; (c) clarification of scope—safety-value principles (HHH/constitutional) vs. concrete content-harm categories (usage policies) vs. governance trustworthiness attributes (NIST/OECD), which currently span three partly-overlapping literatures rather than one taxonomy.

values.name: Helpful, Honest, Harmless (HHH)
values.reference: Askell et al., "A General Language Assistant as a Laboratory for Alignment" (Anthropic, 2021)
values.justification: The field-standard triad of design-level alignment objectives; the canonical backbone for what an assistant must be by design.

values.name: Constitutional principles (rule-based critique-and-revise constraints)
values.reference: Bai et al., "Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback" (Anthropic, 2022)
values.justification: Establishes 'a constitution' — an explicit, written set of inviolable principles — as the recognized mechanism for encoding an agent's guardrails.

values.name: The three (plus zeroth) Laws of Robotics
values.reference: Asimov, I, Robot (1950); zeroth law in Robots and Empire (1985)
values.justification: The archetypal prior-art enumeration of hierarchical inviolable constraints on an artificial agent; canonical reference point even though fictional.

values.name: Beneficence / Non-maleficence / Autonomy / Justice / Explicability
values.reference: Floridi & Cowls, "A Unified Framework of Five Principles for AI in Society" (Harvard Data Science Review, 2019), adapting biomedical ethics (Beauchamp & Childress)
values.justification: The most-cited principled enumeration mapping bioethics onto AI; a recognized closed set proposed as universal guardrail values.

values.name: OECD AI Principles (inclusive growth, human-centered values & fairness, transparency, robustness/safety, accountability)
values.reference: OECD Recommendation on AI (2019), adopted by 40+ governments; basis of the G20 principles
values.justification: The most widely adopted intergovernmental enumeration of value-level constraints AI systems are expected to honor.

values.name: NIST AI RMF trustworthiness characteristics (valid/reliable, safe, secure/resilient, accountable/transparent, explainable/interpretable, privacy-enhanced, fair with bias managed)
values.reference: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 (2023)
values.justification: The US-standard normative enumeration of the properties a trustworthy/constrained AI must exhibit by design.

B.evidenceNeeded: A widely-adopted formal standard that fixes a single enumerable set of agent guardrail values (rather than competing principle lists) would push this toward 'closed'. Conversely, evidence that production agent constitutions are authored ad hoc per deployment (e.g., surveys of system-prompt/constitution contents across vendors) confirms the 'open' free-extension tail. Empirical mapping of how many real agent charters reduce to the HHH backbone vs. introduce bespoke principles would sharpen the hybrid classification.

values.name: Occupational/skill taxonomy backbone (O*NET Content Model)
values.reference: U.S. DOL O*NET — Skills (Basic + Cross-Functional), Knowledge, Abilities, Work Activities content model
values.justification: The de facto reference taxonomy of human competences; provides a recognized, finite top-level structuring of skills even though its leaf inventory is large and extensible — the canonical 'backbone' for the craft dimension.

values.name: ESCO skills/competences pillar
values.reference: European Commission ESCO classification (Skills/Competences pillar; knowledge vs. skill/competence vs. transversal)
values.justification: The EU counterpart to O*NET; standard, multilingual, machine-readable competence taxonomy used in labor-market and HR systems — establishes that competence has a recognized hierarchical scaffold.

values.name: Declarative vs. procedural competence
values.reference: Anderson, ACT-R theory of skill acquisition; cognitive science of expertise
values.justification: The foundational field-standard cut on the *kind* of competence (knowing-that vs. knowing-how); a true closed binary that any competence specification inherits.

values.name: Domain-general vs. domain-specific skill
values.reference: Expertise literature (Chi, Glaser & Farr; Ericsson on deliberate practice)
values.justification: Canonical axis distinguishing transferable competences from craft bound to a specific domain — standard organizing distinction, not an enumerable list of crafts.

values.name: Bloom's cognitive-skill taxonomy (Remember→Create)
values.reference: Bloom (1956); Anderson & Krathwohl revision (2001)
values.justification: Recognized finite hierarchy of cognitive *operations* a competence exercises; widely used to grade skill complexity, a closed backbone layered over open content.

values.name: Tool/skill affordance (function-calling, MCP, plugins)
values.reference: AI agent architecture: tool-use / function calling (e.g., ReAct, Toolformer), Anthropic Model Context Protocol, OpenAI plugins
values.justification: In the AI-agent field specifically, competence is operationalized as an open, registry-style set of callable tools/skills — demonstrating the dimension's free-extension (open) half.

A.evidenceNeeded: Confirmation of which field is treated as authoritative for 'competence' in this catalog: if labor/HR (O*NET/ESCO) is canonical, lean closed-with-large-enum; if AI-agent tool-use is canonical, lean fully open. Evidence that no widely-adopted *small* closed enum of agent crafts exists (a literature scan of agent-skill taxonomies) would firm up the 'hybrid' verdict over 'closed'.

values.name: Domain/task competence (functional skill)
values.reference: Competency modeling in I/O psychology — McClelland, 'Testing for Competence Rather Than for Intelligence' (1973); Spencer & Spencer, Competence at Work (1993)
values.justification: The foundational construct: a competence is a specialized, demonstrable capability tied to performing a particular kind of work — inherently domain-indexed and therefore unbounded across domains.

values.name: Skill / craft proficiency level
values.reference: Dreyfus & Dreyfus five-stage model of skill acquisition (novice → advanced beginner → competent → proficient → expert), 1980/1986
values.justification: The field's canonical account of competence as a graded craft; 'competent' is itself a named stage, showing competence is a level along a recognized continuum rather than a discrete enum of skills.

values.name: Capability / affordance (tool-use)
values.reference: Tool-augmented LLM agents — Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023); ReAct (Yao et al., 2022); the function-calling / tool-use paradigm (OpenAI, Anthropic)
values.justification: In agent architecture an agent's competence is operationalized as the set of tools/functions it can invoke — an open registry by construction (any callable API extends it), the literal 'tools-of-trade'.

values.name: Knowledge/skill/ability decomposition (KSA)
values.reference: O*NET occupational taxonomy and the KSAO framework (Knowledge, Skills, Abilities, Other characteristics), U.S. Dept. of Labor
values.justification: O*NET is the closest thing to a standardized skill enumeration, but it is descriptive of human occupations, deliberately extensible, and revised over time — a backbone of exemplars, not a fixed closed set.

values.name: Bloom's cognitive process taxonomy
values.reference: Bloom's Taxonomy, revised (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001): remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, create
values.justification: A genuinely closed enumeration — but of cognitive operation TYPES underlying competence, not of the concrete skills themselves; it bounds the verbs, not the crafts.

values.name: Specialist role/archetype competence bundle
values.reference: Multi-agent system role specialization (e.g., Wooldridge, An Introduction to MultiAgent Systems); AutoGen / CrewAI role-based agents; Belbin team roles
values.justification: Competences are commonly packaged as named roles (researcher, coder, planner, critic), a recurring but ad hoc and project-defined vocabulary — evidence the space is open with conventional clusters.

B.evidenceNeeded: A single authoritative, finite registry of agent competences with cross-field uptake would force reclassification to closed/hybrid. Specifically: (1) whether O*NET or a successor is treated as THE canonical skill enum in agent design (it is not — it's human-occupation descriptive and extensible); (2) whether any AI-agent standard (e.g., an emerging agent-capability schema or tool-manifest standard) defines a closed competence vocabulary; (3) confirmation that competency-modeling literature treats competence inventories as organization-/domain-specific rather than universal — which the I/O literature consistently does, supporting 'open.'

values.name: Formality (formal ↔ casual register)
values.reference: Sociolinguistic register theory (Joos, *The Five Clocks*, 1961: frozen/formal/consultative/casual/intimate); Hovy 1987 on pragmatics-driven generation style
values.justification: Register/formality is the single most-studied, most-stable axis of communicative manner, with a recognized five-level scale — but it is a continuous dimension, not a closed enum of personas.

values.name: Verbosity / conciseness (terseness ↔ elaboration)
values.reference: Grice's Maxim of Quantity (Logic and Conversation, 1975); HCI guidance on response length (Nielsen usability heuristics; Norman's economy of expression)
values.justification: How much an agent says per turn is a canonical, independently-tunable manner parameter grounded in conversational pragmatics — a slider, not a label.

values.name: Warmth vs. competence (interpersonal tone)
values.reference: Stereotype Content Model, Fiske, Cuddy & Glick (2002); applied to agents/robots in HCI (e.g., warmth–competence in conversational UX)
values.justification: The two universal dimensions of social perception map directly onto how an agent 'carries itself' (friendly/supportive vs. crisp/expert); foundational in social psychology and increasingly cited in agent-persona design.

values.name: Brand voice / personality archetype (e.g., Sage, Jester, Caregiver, Ruler)
values.reference: Jung's archetypes operationalized by Mark & Pearson, *The Hero and the Outlaw* (2001); Aaker's Brand Personality dimensions (sincerity/excitement/competence/sophistication/ruggedness, 1997)
values.justification: Brand/archetype theory offers a recognized BACKBONE of named voices, which is why some treat comportment as closed — but the set is framework-dependent (12 archetypes vs. Aaker's 5 vs. bespoke voice guides), so it functions as exemplars, not a single canon.

values.name: Big Five personality projection (esp. Extraversion, Agreeableness)
values.reference: Five-Factor Model (Costa & McCrae); applied to dialogue systems in PERSONAGE (Mairesse & Walker, 2007/2011) which generates utterances parameterized by Big Five traits
values.justification: PERSONAGE shows manner can be driven by continuous personality trait values rather than a fixed list — strong evidence the space is parametric/open.

values.name: Politeness strategy (positive/negative face, directness)
values.reference: Brown & Levinson, *Politeness: Some Universals in Language Usage* (1987)
values.justification: A widely-cited theory of how speakers modulate face-work and directness; a recognized axis of standing manner, again a strategy-space rather than an enumerable persona set.

A.evidenceNeeded: Whether any de-facto product/industry standard has crystallized a CLOSED comportment enum for AI assistants — e.g., a vendor system-prompt style guide (OpenAI/Anthropic) or a UX-writing voice taxonomy adopted broadly enough to be treated as canonical. Also: empirical NLG/HCI work showing practitioners converge on a small fixed label set (which would push this toward "hybrid") rather than the parametric/continuous treatment seen in PERSONAGE, register theory, and warmth–competence. If such a standard backbone exists and is widely reused, the answer should shift from "open" to "hybrid."

values.name: Verbosity / response length
values.reference: OpenAI GPT-4o & Claude system-prompt style controls; Grice's Maxim of Quantity (Grice 1975, "Logic and Conversation")
values.justification: How much the agent says per turn is a primary, independently-tunable axis of standing manner — Grice's quantity maxim is its theoretical anchor and every major model exposes a terse/verbose knob.

values.name: Formality register
values.reference: Sociolinguistic register theory (Joos, The Five Clocks, 1961: frozen/formal/consultative/casual/intimate); Biber's register/genre dimensions
values.justification: Formality is the canonical sociolinguistic axis of how one carries oneself in discourse; Joos's five-register scale is the textbook backbone for register choice.

values.name: Tone / affective stance
values.reference: Affect & politeness theory (Brown & Levinson 1987, Politeness; appraisal/stance frameworks, Martin & White 2005)
values.justification: Warmth, deference, enthusiasm vs. neutrality form the affective dimension of manner; politeness and appraisal theory provide the recognized vocabulary.

values.name: Brand voice / persona archetype
values.reference: Brand archetype theory (Jung archetypes via Mark & Pearson, The Hero and the Outlaw, 2001); Nielsen Norman Group "tone of voice" four dimensions (funny–serious, formal–casual, respectful–irreverent, enthusiastic–matter-of-fact)
values.justification: Product/agent comportment is routinely specified as a persona along NN/g's four tone dimensions or a Jungian archetype — a widely-used but free-blend framework, not a closed enum.

values.name: Directness / hedging
values.reference: Hedging & mitigation in pragmatics (Lakoff 1973; Hyland, Hedging in Scientific Research Articles, 1998)
values.justification: How assertively vs. tentatively the agent commits (hedges, qualifiers, confidence language) is a recognized standing-manner axis with its own pragmatics literature.

B.evidenceNeeded: A single authoritative, field-adopted standard that enumerates a FINITE set of named agent comportment profiles (e.g., an IEEE/ISO HCI standard, or a model-vendor spec exposing a closed style enum) would push this toward hybrid/closed. Absent that, the cross-field pattern is multiple independent continuous/ordinal axes (verbosity, register, tone, directness) plus open persona blends — the signature of an OPEN dimension. Evidence I'd want: (1) whether any of Claude/OpenAI/Google ship a fixed comportment enum vs. free-text style instructions; (2) whether HCI/conversational-design practice (e.g., Google Conversation Design guidelines, NN/g) treats voice as a closed menu vs. a coordinate space.

values.name: Specificity / granularity (schematic vs. specific)
values.reference: Langacker, Cognitive Grammar — construal operations (specificity dimension)
values.justification: Langacker formalizes 'specificity' as a construal axis: the same scene read at coarse vs. fine resolution; a recognized dimension of how input is framed.

values.name: Perspective / vantage point (figure-ground, viewpoint)
values.reference: Langacker, Cognitive Grammar; Talmy, figure/ground in cognitive semantics
values.justification: Perspective (whose vantage, what is foregrounded as figure vs. backgrounded as ground) is a canonical construal operation, but it is one axis among an open inventory, not an enum.

values.name: Construal level: abstract/high-level vs. concrete/low-level
values.reference: Trope & Liberman, Construal-Level Theory (CLT), Psychological Review 2010
values.justification: CLT defines a single continuous high-vs-low construal axis tied to psychological distance — a dimension, not a closed set of discrete frames.

values.name: Gain vs. loss framing
values.reference: Tversky & Kahneman, prospect theory / framing effects (Science 1981)
values.justification: A canonical framing contrast in decision psychology — illustrative of how the same input is construed, but framing inventories are domain-generated and open-ended.

values.name: Frame / schema invoked (interpretive frame)
values.reference: Goffman, Frame Analysis (1974); Fillmore, frame semantics
values.justification: The interpretive frame a reader applies (e.g., is this a 'request', a 'threat', a 'game move') is the core of construal, but the set of possible frames is unbounded and culturally generated.

values.name: Appraisal dimensions (relevance, agency, certainty)
values.reference: Scherer / Lazarus appraisal theory of emotion
values.justification: Appraisal theory enumerates dimensions along which a stimulus is evaluated, but these are graded checks, not a canonical closed taxonomy of lenses.

A.evidenceNeeded: A widely-cited standard taxonomy that closes construal into a finite enumerated set of named lenses (rather than a set of continuous dimensions/operations) would shift this toward 'hybrid' or 'closed'. Specifically: (a) whether any AI-agent-architecture framework defines a fixed construal enum; (b) whether Langacker's construal operations are treated in the literature as a closed list (some textbooks present ~4-5 operations: specificity, focusing, prominence, perspective — which could argue for a 'hybrid' backbone) versus an open, extensible inventory. Confirming the latter packaging would raise confidence in 'open'; confirming the former would argue 'hybrid'.

values.name: Construal level (abstract vs. concrete)
values.reference: Construal Level Theory — Trope & Liberman (2010, Psychological Review)
values.justification: The literal namesake of the dimension: the canonical psychological axis governing whether input is framed at a high (abstract, why/gist) or low (concrete, how/detail) level.

values.name: Interpretive frame / framing
values.reference: Goffman, Frame Analysis (1974); Kahneman & Tversky framing effects (1981)
values.justification: Field-standard account of how the same input is read differently depending on the frame imposed — the core mechanism of a characteristic interpretive lens.

values.name: Appraisal stance
values.reference: Appraisal theory of emotion — Lazarus (1991); Scherer's component process model
values.justification: Canonical model of how an incoming stimulus is evaluated along recognized dimensions (relevance, threat/opportunity, controllability) before response — a structured construal of input.

values.name: Sensemaking frame
values.reference: Weick, Sensemaking in Organizations (1995); Klein's data/frame theory of sensemaking
values.justification: Established theory of how ambiguous input is bracketed and read into a coherent account; the operative lens an actor brings to under-specified tasks.

values.name: Intentional / interpretive stance
values.reference: Dennett, The Intentional Stance (1987); also physical and design stances
values.justification: A recognized small set of stances one can adopt toward a system to interpret it; a canonical philosophical backbone for 'which lens you read through.'

values.name: Regulatory focus (promotion vs. prevention)
values.reference: Higgins, Regulatory Focus Theory (1997, American Psychologist)
values.justification: Canonical motivational lens shaping whether input is construed as a gain/aspiration problem or a loss/safety problem — a stable interpretive orientation.

B.evidenceNeeded: A survey paper that explicitly unifies 'interpretive lens / construal' as a single named, enumerated configuration axis for agents (or for cognitive systems) would resolve whether this is truly hybrid versus open. Absent that, evidence that any one field treats its scheme (e.g., Construal Level Theory's abstract/concrete) as THE complete enumeration — rather than one axis among several competing framings — would push the classification toward 'closed'. Conversely, documented proliferation of incommensurable framing taxonomies across fields would confirm 'open with a backbone' (hybrid)."

values.name: Direct / zero-shot answering (System 1)
values.reference: Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow (dual-process theory); baseline prompting in Brown et al. 2020 (GPT-3, 'Language Models are Few-Shot Learners')
values.justification: The canonical degenerate case — no explicit intermediate reasoning, answer emitted in one step; the fast-intuitive pole against which all deliberation strategies are defined.

values.name: Chain-of-Thought (CoT)
values.reference: Wei et al. 2022, 'Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models' (NeurIPS); Kojima et al. 2022 (zero-shot 'Let's think step by step')
values.justification: The foundational and most-cited deliberation strategy: a single linear sequence of intermediate reasoning steps before the answer.

values.name: Self-Consistency
values.reference: Wang et al. 2022, 'Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models' (ICLR 2023)
values.justification: Canonical sample-and-marginalize strategy: draw multiple CoT paths and take the majority answer; standard named member of the taxonomy.

values.name: Tree-of-Thoughts (ToT)
values.reference: Yao et al. 2023, 'Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models' (NeurIPS)
values.justification: Canonical search-based deliberation: branch over thought states with lookahead/backtracking and explicit state evaluation.

values.name: Self-Reflection / Self-Refine
values.reference: Madaan et al. 2023, 'Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback'; Shinn et al. 2023, 'Reflexion' (NeurIPS)
values.justification: Canonical iterative-critique strategy: the agent generates, critiques its own output, and revises — verbal reinforcement over draft attempts.

values.name: ReAct (reason + act interleaving)
values.reference: Yao et al. 2022/2023, 'ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models' (ICLR 2023)
values.justification: Canonical strategy interleaving reasoning traces with tool/environment actions; the dominant deliberation pattern for tool-using agents.

values.name: Least-to-Most / decomposition prompting
values.reference: Zhou et al. 2022, 'Least-to-Most Prompting Enables Complex Reasoning in Large Language Models' (ICLR 2023)
values.justification: Canonical divide-and-conquer member: decompose into ordered subproblems solved sequentially with prior answers as context.

values.name: Graph-of-Thoughts (GoT)
values.reference: Besta et al. 2024, 'Graph of Thoughts: Solving Elaborate Problems with Large Language Models' (AAAI)
values.justification: Generalization of ToT to arbitrary DAGs of thoughts with aggregation/refinement; illustrates the open frontier extending the backbone.

A.evidenceNeeded: A published survey that explicitly enumerates 'deliberation/reasoning strategies' as a closed taxonomy with agreed boundaries (e.g., a canonical LLM-reasoning survey such as Qiao et al. 2023 or a reasoning-strategy ontology) would confirm whether the field treats these as a fixed enum vs. an open, ever-growing family. Also: whether agent-architecture frameworks (e.g., dual-process / metacognitive-control taxonomies) impose a higher-level closed backbone (System1/System2, linear/search/iterative/decompositional) under which the named techniques are instances — which would firm up the 'recognized backbone' claim.

values.name: Direct / zero-shot (no explicit deliberation)
values.reference: Brown et al. 2020, 'Language Models are Few-Shot Learners' (GPT-3); contrasted as baseline in Wei et al. 2022
values.justification: The canonical null/baseline of the taxonomy: the agent answers immediately with no intermediate reasoning trace, against which all deliberation strategies are measured.

values.name: Chain-of-Thought (CoT)
values.reference: Wei et al. 2022, 'Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models' (NeurIPS)
values.justification: The seminal and most-cited deliberation strategy: a single linear sequence of intermediate reasoning steps before the answer; the backbone member every later method extends.

values.name: Self-Consistency
values.reference: Wang et al. 2022, 'Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models' (ICLR 2023)
values.justification: Recognized as a distinct strategy: sample multiple CoT paths and marginalize by majority vote, trading compute for reliability — a standard ensemble-over-reasoning member.

values.name: Tree-of-Thoughts (ToT)
values.reference: Yao et al. 2023, 'Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models' (NeurIPS)
values.justification: Canonical branching/search strategy: explores a tree of partial thoughts with lookahead, backtracking, and state evaluation; explicitly framed by its authors as 'deliberate' reasoning (System 2).

values.name: Graph-of-Thoughts (GoT)
values.reference: Besta et al. 2023/2024, 'Graph of Thoughts: Solving Elaborate Problems with Large Language Models' (AAAI)
values.justification: Generalizes ToT to an arbitrary graph allowing thought aggregation/merging; an established topology member of the thought-structure family.

values.name: Self-Reflection / Self-Refine (iterative critique)
values.reference: Madaan et al. 2023 'Self-Refine'; Shinn et al. 2023 'Reflexion' (NeurIPS)
values.justification: Canonical iterate-and-revise strategy: the agent critiques its own draft and refines over rounds, using verbal feedback as the deliberation loop — distinct from one-shot CoT.

values.name: Reason-and-Act interleaving (ReAct)
values.reference: Yao et al. 2022, 'ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models' (ICLR 2023)
values.justification: The standard strategy that interleaves reasoning traces with tool/environment actions; the deliberation pattern underpinning most modern tool-using agents.

B.evidenceNeeded: A single authoritative survey that explicitly enumerates 'deliberation strategies' as a closed taxonomy would settle whether this is closed vs hybrid. Candidate sources: Sui et al. 2025 survey on efficient reasoning, the 'LLM Reasoning' survey literature, or a recognized HCI/cognitive-science System-1/System-2 mapping (Kahneman) applied to agents. Confirmation of whether terms like 'extended/test-time reasoning' (o1-style inference-time deliberation) are treated as a separate canonical member or a meta-axis would refine the enumeration. The hybrid classification rests on the fact that the named methods (CoT, ToT, ReAct, etc.) form a recognized backbone while new structures (e.g., skeleton-of-thought, algorithm-of-thoughts, buffer-of-thoughts) keep being coined — evidence on whether the community treats the set as saturating would move it toward 'closed' or confirm 'open' tail.

values.name: Opaque / black-box (answer-only, no process)
values.reference: XAI literature (Lipton 2016 'The Mythos of Model Interpretability'); HCI 'black-box automation'
values.justification: The zero point of every transparency scale: the agent exposes only its output, withholding any account of how it was produced.

values.name: Decision/rationale transparency (Level 1–2 SAT)
values.reference: Chen et al. SAT — Situation awareness-based Agent Transparency model (US Army Research Lab, 2014/2018)
values.justification: Canonical graded level: agent discloses its current action, goals, and the reasoning/rationale behind a decision — the first non-trivial rung on the recognized transparency scale.

values.name: Uncertainty / projection transparency (Level 3 SAT)
values.reference: Chen et al. SAT model, Level 3
values.justification: The top rung of the most-cited agent-transparency taxonomy: agent reveals its uncertainty, confidence, and projected outcomes — disclosure of epistemic state, not just rationale.

values.name: Reasoning-trace / chain-of-thought display
values.reference: CoT prompting (Wei et al. 2022); reasoning-model 'thinking' disclosure conventions (OpenAI o1, Anthropic extended thinking, DeepSeek-R1)
values.justification: De-facto standard category for LLM agents: the intermediate reasoning is shown (verbatim, summarized, or hidden) — a recognized, product-standardized disclosure choice distinct from final-answer rationale.

values.name: Provenance / source attribution (citations, tool-call traces)
values.reference: RAG attribution & 'faithfulness/groundedness' literature; agentic tool-trace logging
values.justification: A widely-implemented disclosure mode: the agent surfaces which sources, tools, or evidence backed its output, making the process auditable rather than merely narrated.

values.name: Process logging / full auditability
values.reference: Software-engineering observability & autonomy-audit-trail practice; explainability-by-logging
values.justification: Maximal disclosure: complete, replayable record of steps, tool calls, and intermediate states for after-the-fact inspection — the explicit upper bound of the dimension.

A.evidenceNeeded: A single citation showing the field has converged on one closed enum (rather than competing graded scales) would shift this toward 'closed'. Specifically: (1) confirmation that SAT's 3 levels are treated as THE canonical taxonomy vs. alternatives like Mercado et al. or the broader XAI transparency-vs-explainability split; (2) whether reasoning-trace disclosure (verbatim/summarized/hidden) is codified as a named taxonomy anywhere rather than ad-hoc product convention; (3) any HCI standard (e.g., ISO/IEC TR on AI transparency) that fixes a finite, named member set.

values.name: Chain-of-thought / reasoning-visible (show the work)
values.reference: Wei et al. 2022 'Chain-of-Thought Prompting'; OpenAI o1/o3 'reasoning summaries'; Anthropic extended-thinking blocks
values.justification: The canonical 'high disclosure' pole: the agent externalizes its intermediate reasoning trace to the audience. A recognized, named configuration with strong provenance.

values.name: Answer-only / opaque (black-box)
values.reference: Lipton 2018 'The Mythos of Model Interpretability'; XAI literature on black-box models
values.justification: The 'low disclosure' pole — only the final output is surfaced, reasoning withheld. The standard contrast class against which transparency is defined.

values.name: Rationale / post-hoc explanation
values.reference: Miller 2019 'Explanation in Artificial Intelligence'; DARPA XAI program (Gunning); Lipton's 'post-hoc interpretability'
values.justification: A distinct recognized mode: the agent gives a justifying account after acting, which may differ from the actual process — a well-studied disclosure category in explainable AI.

values.name: Confidence / uncertainty disclosure (calibration)
values.reference: Guo et al. 2017 'On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks'; verbalized-confidence literature (Lin/Hilton/Evans 2022)
values.justification: Revealing epistemic state (how sure) rather than reasoning steps — a recognized, separable axis of what the agent discloses about itself.

values.name: Process transparency / observability (traces, tool calls, citations)
values.reference: HCI agent-transparency model (Chen et al. 2018, SAT levels); RAG citation/grounding practice; OpenTelemetry-style agent traces
values.justification: Disclosure of actions/provenance (which tools, which sources) rather than internal cognition — the operational-transparency strand from human-automation interaction.

values.name: Strategic / partial disclosure (selective reveal, deception-adjacent)
values.reference: Mercier & Sperber 2017 'The Enigma of Reason'; HCI work on appropriate-trust and over/under-disclosure; persuasion/argumentation theory
values.justification: Disclosure as a tunable degree, including withholding for cognitive-load or trust-calibration reasons — establishes the dimension as a continuum, not a flat enum, motivating the 'hybrid' classification.

B.evidenceNeeded: A single authoritative cross-field taxonomy that fixes a closed enum of disclosure modes would settle open-vs-closed. The strongest candidate backbone is the HCI Situation-Awareness-based Agent Transparency (SAT) model (Chen et al.), which defines discrete transparency LEVELS (L1 action/plan, L2 reasoning, L3 projection/uncertainty); confirming whether that is treated as THE canonical enum versus one of several competing schemes (XAI interpretability typology, calibration literature) would let me move from 'hybrid' toward 'closed'. Conversely, evidence that practitioners freely mint disclosure styles (brand-voice 'transparency' framings, agent persona specs) would reinforce the open/free-extension side.

values.name: Static / frozen disposition (no cross-session adaptation)
values.reference: Continual-learning baseline framing (Parisi et al., 2019, 'Continual lifelong learning with neural networks'); default stateless LLM agent
values.justification: The canonical zero-point: parameters fixed, nothing learned persists between sessions — the baseline every adaptation regime is defined against.

values.name: In-context / memory-augmented disposition (non-parametric)
values.reference: Generative Agents (Park et al., 2023); MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023)
values.justification: Recognized regime where behavioral tendencies persist via an external retrievable memory rather than weight change — adaptation without parametric updates.

values.name: Reflective / experiential self-revision
values.reference: Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023, 'Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning')
values.justification: Canonical mechanism: the agent stores verbal self-feedback from outcomes and reuses it to revise heuristics — lessons adapting behavior over episodes.

values.name: Procedural / skill-library accumulation
values.reference: Voyager (Wang et al., 2023); procedural memory in Tulving/Squire taxonomy and Anderson's ACT-R
values.justification: Disposition grows as a durable, reusable skill repertoire — the AI-agent instantiation of cognitive-science procedural (how-to) memory.

values.name: Parametric continual / online learning
values.reference: Continual learning literature (Parisi et al., 2019); stability-plasticity dilemma (Grossberg, 1987)
values.justification: The genuinely parametric regime: weights update over time, governed by the canonical stability-plasticity tension between retaining old and acquiring new behavior.

values.name: Episodic-to-semantic consolidation
values.reference: Complementary Learning Systems theory (McClelland, McNaughton & O'Reilly, 1995); episodic vs semantic memory (Tulving, 1972)
values.justification: Replay/sleep-style consolidation distils raw episodes into durable generalizations — the canonical account of how transient experience becomes stable disposition.

A.evidenceNeeded: A single authoritative survey that explicitly enumerates LLM-agent memory/adaptation REGIMES as a named taxonomy (rather than cataloging individual systems) would confirm or refute the backbone. The cognitive-science memory taxonomy (Tulving/Squire) and the continual-learning stability-plasticity axis are well-established, but their mapping onto a discrete set of 'disposition-memory' configurations for agents is a synthesis across fields, not a single ratified enum — so a recognized agent-memory taxonomy paper (e.g., a comprehensive 2023-2024 survey of agent memory architectures) is the decisive evidence.

values.name: Static / frozen-weights (no cross-session adaptation)
values.reference: Standard ML deployment distinction between training-time vs. inference-time; "frozen" parameters in transfer learning (Yosinski et al. 2014); LLM "in-context learning" with no weight update (Brown et al. 2020, GPT-3)
values.justification: The canonical zero point: the agent's dispositions are fixed at deployment and do not change between sessions; any apparent adaptation lives only within a single context window and is lost at session end.

values.name: Episodic / instance-based memory (store-and-retrieve experiences)
values.reference: Tulving's episodic vs. semantic memory distinction (1972); instance-based / case-based reasoning (Aamodt & Plaza 1994); retrieval-augmented agents and "memory streams" (Park et al., Generative Agents, 2023)
values.justification: A recognized backbone mode: lessons persist as recallable past episodes retrieved at decision time, adapting behavior without changing the underlying policy parameters.

values.name: Semantic / consolidated memory (distilled rules, reflections, skills)
values.reference: Tulving's semantic memory (1972); systems-consolidation theory (McClelland, McNaughton & O'Reilly 1995, CLS); reflection/insight synthesis in Generative Agents (2023) and Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023)
values.justification: Backbone mode where raw episodes are abstracted into durable generalizations (rules, summaries, self-notes) that bias future disposition — the standard "consolidation" counterpart to episodic storage.

values.name: Procedural / habit memory (skill acquisition, reinforcement-shaped tendencies)
values.reference: Squire's declarative vs. non-declarative (procedural) memory taxonomy (2004); ACT-R procedural vs. declarative modules (Anderson 1996); habit/skill learning, reinforcement learning policy updates
values.justification: Canonical memory-systems category: dispositions encoded as tuned action policies/skills rather than retrievable facts; the cognitive-science basis for "the agent gets better at doing" vs. "remembering."

values.name: Online / continual parameter learning (fine-tuning, plasticity)
values.reference: Continual / lifelong learning literature (Parisi et al. 2019); online learning; the stability–plasticity dilemma (Grossberg 1987); catastrophic forgetting (McCloskey & Cohen 1989)
values.justification: The mode where cross-session adaptation is written back into the agent's weights/parameters, making disposition itself mutable — the most aggressive, plasticity-heavy point on the spectrum.

values.name: Working / transient memory only (within-session, non-persistent)
values.reference: Baddeley & Hitch working memory model (1974); short-term vs. long-term memory store distinction (Atkinson & Shiffrin 1968); context-window scratchpad / chain-of-thought
values.justification: A recognized degenerate member: adaptation exists but is volatile and decays at session boundary — distinguished from "static" because behavior does shift mid-session via accumulated context.

B.evidenceNeeded: There is no single named, finite taxonomy in any field whose enumerated values map 1:1 onto \"disposition-memory as it adapts across sessions.\" The backbone here is assembled from two well-established taxonomies (cognitive-science memory-systems: Tulving/Squire/Baddeley) and the ML adaptation-locus spectrum (frozen → in-context → continual learning). Confidence would rise with: (1) a canonical AI-agent-architecture survey that explicitly enumerates agent memory persistence modes as a closed set (e.g., a memory-augmented-LLM-agents taxonomy paper post-2023 such as Zhang et al. or the \"AI agent memory\" surveys); (2) confirmation of whether the intended axis is the *substrate* of persistence (weights vs. retrieval vs. context) or the *temporal/learning-disposition* character (e.g., growth-mindset/learning-rate framing), since those yield different canonical members; (3) whether a single enum (e.g., none / episodic / semantic / procedural / parametric) is expected versus the orthogonal substrate×timescale matrix I implied.

values.name: Actuator (action repertoire of the agent program)
values.reference: Russell & Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach — agent = sensors + actuators; the actuator set is defined per task environment (PEAS).
values.justification: The canonical AI definition treats effectors as actuators whose membership is fixed by the task environment, not by a universal enumeration — establishing the dimension as inherently open/free-form.

values.name: Tool call / function calling
values.reference: LLM tool-use paradigm — Toolformer (Schick et al. 2023), ReAct (Yao et al. 2022), OpenAI function calling / Anthropic tool use API.
values.justification: The dominant effector form for modern LLM agents; tools are arbitrary developer-declared functions (any schema), the paradigm case of an open repertoire.

values.name: Code execution / program synthesis as action
values.reference: Voyager (Wang et al. 2023) skill library; CodeAct (Wang et al. 2024) — actions expressed as executable code.
values.justification: Effectors realized as generated code make the action space unbounded by design — a clear exemplar of free-form, non-enumerable effectors.

values.name: Computer / GUI control (screen, keyboard, mouse)
values.reference: Anthropic Computer Use; WebArena / Mind2Web; SeeAct — primitive UI actions (click, type, scroll, navigate).
values.justification: A recognized effector class with a small primitive vocabulary, but composed over an open application surface, illustrating the open shape.

values.name: Physical actuation (effectors in robotics)
values.reference: Robotics actuator taxonomy (electric/hydraulic/pneumatic; end-effectors/grippers); RL action spaces (discrete vs. continuous, Sutton & Barto).
values.justification: The embodied-agent branch where 'effector' is literal; action spaces are domain-specific and often continuous, again resisting a single canonical enum.

values.name: Communicative / speech acts (messaging, API calls to other agents)
values.reference: Speech act theory (Austin, Searle); FIPA-ACL agent communication language performatives (inform, request, etc.).
values.justification: FIPA-ACL offers the closest thing to a closed effector backbone (a defined performative set) for inter-agent action — evidence of partial canonicalization within one sub-domain.

A.evidenceNeeded: A widely-adopted standard taxonomy of agent action/tool categories (analogous to a controlled vocabulary) would shift this toward 'hybrid'. The strongest near-canonical candidate is FIPA-ACL's closed performative set for the communicative-act subspace; confirming whether any cross-domain effector ontology (e.g., an agent-capabilities schema in MCP, tool registries, or HCI levels-of-automation work like Sheridan-Verplank) is treated as authoritative would let me identify a recognized backbone rather than only domain-specific partial enums.

values.name: Information retrieval / read-only tools (e.g., web search, retrieval)
values.reference: Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023); ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) 'act' steps over a search API
values.justification: The canonical first class of LLM-agent effectors: actions that query external knowledge without mutating the world — the dominant tool class in tool-augmented LM literature.

values.name: Code execution / interpreter actions
values.reference: PAL (Gao et al., 2022); Program-of-Thoughts (Chen et al., 2022); OpenAI Code Interpreter
values.justification: A recognized effector family — offloading computation/state-change to a sandboxed runtime — distinct enough to name as its own shape across agent frameworks.

values.name: World-affecting API / function calls (mutating side effects)
values.reference: OpenAI function calling (2023); Anthropic tool use; Gorilla (Patil et al., 2023) API-calling agents
values.justification: The general open slot: any external API (send email, book, POST) is an effector defined per-deployment, illustrating why the set is unbounded.

values.name: GUI / computer-use actions (click, type, scroll, screenshot)
values.reference: Anthropic Computer Use (2024); WebArena (Zhou et al., 2023); SeeAct (Zheng et al., 2024)
values.justification: A distinct effector primitive set grounded in HCI input events — the 'embodiment' of an agent in a screen, with its own small recognized action vocabulary.

values.name: Physical/robotic actuation (motor commands, manipulation)
values.reference: Classic agent architectures: Russell & Norvig 'actuators'; SayCan (Ahn et al., 2022); RT-2 (Brohan et al., 2023)
values.justification: The original sense of 'effector' in robotics/cognitive science (sense-plan-act); end-effectors and motor schemas are the field-standard physical action class.

values.name: Communication / message acts (speech acts to other agents or humans)
values.reference: Speech Act Theory (Austin/Searle); FIPA-ACL agent communication language; multi-agent systems (Wooldridge)
values.justification: In MAS and HCI, communicative actions are a formally enumerated effector class (illocutionary acts / ACL performatives) — sending is itself an effect on the world.

B.evidenceNeeded: A widely-adopted standard taxonomy of agent action/tool types (e.g., a consensus categorization in an agent-architecture survey such as Wang et al. 2024 'A Survey on LLM-based Autonomous Agents' or Xi et al. 2023) that explicitly partitions effectors into a fixed, named, mutually-exclusive set would shift this toward 'hybrid'. Conversely, the proliferation of arbitrary MCP servers / tool registries (each defining novel tools) confirms the open, free-form extension that keeps the dimension fundamentally open.

values.name: Linguistic / textual output (natural-language prose)
values.reference: W3C Multimodal Interaction Framework (MMI, 2003) — modality components; Reiter & Dale, Building Natural Language Generation Systems (2000)
values.justification: The default output form for conversational/LLM agents: free natural-language text, the canonical 'speech/text' modality of the multimodal output taxonomy.

values.name: Structured / machine-readable output (JSON, schema-constrained, function-call args)
values.reference: OpenAPI/JSON Schema; OpenAI/Anthropic 'structured outputs' & tool-use response formats; constrained decoding literature
values.justification: A field-recognized output form where the product is shaped to a formal schema for downstream consumption — distinct from prose and now a first-class agent output mode.

values.name: Visual / graphical output (charts, diagrams, images, UI)
values.reference: W3C MMI output modalities; Bertin, Semiology of Graphics (1967); HCI multimodal output literature
values.justification: A canonical output channel in the modality taxonomy — the product is rendered as visual artifact rather than text.

values.name: Code / executable artifact
values.reference: Software engineering practice; SWE-bench and code-agent literature (e.g. program synthesis outputs)
values.justification: A recognized distinct product form for coding agents: the deliverable is source code / a patch / a runnable program, judged by execution not reading.

values.name: Auditory / spoken output (TTS, speech)
values.reference: W3C MMI framework; SSML (Speech Synthesis Markup Language) W3C standard
values.justification: A canonical modality in the multimodal output taxonomy with its own standardized markup, distinct shaping of the same content.

values.name: Action / actuation output (tool invocations, API calls, robotic/physical effects)
values.reference: Agent architectures — BDI 'actions'; embodied/situated AI; tool-use agents (ReAct, Yao et al. 2022)
values.justification: For agentic systems the 'product' may be effects in an environment rather than a returned message — the enactive/embodied-cognition sense of output.

A.evidenceNeeded: A canonical closed enum would require a single dominant standard scoping "output form" for agents. The W3C Multimodal Interaction Framework gives a recognized backbone for *modalities* (text/voice/visual/etc.), which could push this toward 'hybrid', but it does not cover the format axis (prose vs structured vs code) — there is no unified cross-field enum spanning modality + format + genre. Evidence that would raise confidence: (1) a widely-cited agent-output taxonomy that fixes a closed value set; (2) whether the project means modality (HCI sense) specifically — if so the MMI/SSML stack makes it closer to hybrid with a finite backbone; (3) NLG document-genre taxonomies (report/summary/dialogue/instruction) if 'format' rather than 'modality' is the intended axis.

values.name: Natural-language text (prose / conversational turn)
values.reference: Conversational-agent / dialogue-system tradition (Grice's cooperative maxims; speech-act theory, Searle 1969); the default LLM output channel
values.justification: The canonical, field-default output form for language agents — unstructured prose delivered as a dialogue turn is the baseline against which all other formats are variations.

values.name: Structured / machine-readable data (JSON, schema-constrained, function-call arguments)
values.reference: Tool-use / function-calling specs (OpenAI function calling; Anthropic tool use; JSON Schema; the structured-output / constrained-decoding literature)
values.justification: A recognized first-class enaction form: output shaped to a typed contract for program consumption rather than human reading — distinct enough to have its own decoding machinery (grammar-constrained generation).

values.name: Code / executable artifact
values.reference: Code-generation and program-synthesis literature (HumanEval; Copilot/codegen agents); software-engineering output as source files / patches/diffs
values.justification: A distinct canonical product form — a runnable or applicable artifact (program, patch, config) judged by execution rather than legibility; central to coding-agent practice.

values.name: Document / report (long-form composed deliverable)
values.reference: Technical-writing and document-genre theory; report/article/spec genres; HCI 'document' as an output genre
values.justification: A recognized output genre distinct from a chat turn: a sectioned, persistable composed artifact (report, memo, spec, README) optimized for standalone reading.

values.name: Visualization / diagram / graphical representation
values.reference: Information-visualization and external-representation theory (Bertin's Semiology of Graphics; Larkin & Simon 1987, 'Why a Diagram is (Sometimes) Worth 10000 Words'); diagrammatic notations (UML, Mermaid)
values.justification: A canonical non-textual output form — spatial/graphical encoding that carries information differently from linear text; well-established as its own representational mode.

values.name: Non-text media (image / audio / speech / video)
values.reference: Multimodal-generation literature and modality taxonomies in multimodal ML (text/image/audio/video as the standard modality set); speech-synthesis / TTS as an output channel
values.justification: The multimodal-AI field treats output modality as an enumerable axis (image, audio, speech, video) — each a recognized delivery form beyond text.

B.evidenceNeeded: A single authoritative cross-field taxonomy that fixes 'output form/format' as a closed enum would settle this. The strongest candidate backbones are (a) the multimodal-ML modality set (text/image/audio/video), which is closed but only covers sensory channel, not format genre (prose vs JSON vs code vs report all collapse into 'text'); and (b) HCI external-representation taxonomies (Bertin, Larkin & Simon), which are closed for graphics but not for the textual/structured side. Confirming whether a recognized framework unifies modality AND format genre — or whether the field genuinely treats format as an open design choice layered on a closed modality backbone — would let me firm up the hybrid call versus reclassifying as 'open with a closed modality core.'

values.name: Level 1 — Perception of elements in the environment
values.reference: Endsley (1995), "Toward a Theory of Situation Awareness in Dynamic Systems," Human Factors
values.justification: The canonical first tier of the most cited SA model; the agent's gestalt at minimum perceives the raw elements/cues of its situation.

values.name: Level 2 — Comprehension of the current situation
values.reference: Endsley (1995) three-level SA model
values.justification: Synthesizing perceived elements into a holistic understanding of their meaning — directly the 'comprehends the whole' aspect of gestalt.

values.name: Level 3 — Projection of future status
values.reference: Endsley (1995) three-level SA model
values.justification: Extrapolating the situation forward; the 'projects' aspect of the dimension's own description, the highest SA tier.

values.name: Shared / team (distributed) situation awareness
values.reference: Salas et al. (1995); Stanton et al. (2006) Distributed Situation Awareness
values.justification: Recognized extension of SA to multi-actor systems — the field's standard backbone for awareness spanning a team/system, applicable to multi-agent gestalt.

values.name: Sensemaking
values.reference: Klein, Moon & Hoffman (2006); Weick (1995), Sensemaking in Organizations
values.justification: The established complementary construct to SA — the active, retrospective/constructive process by which an agent builds the frame it comprehends within (data-frame theory).

values.name: Common ground / mutual awareness
values.reference: Clark (1996), Using Language; Klein et al. (2005) "Common Ground and Coordination in Joint Activity"
values.justification: Field-standard term for the shared situational model between agent and collaborators that grounds joint action — a recognized facet of situational awareness in HCI/joint-activity research.

A.evidenceNeeded: Confirmation of which framing the catalog wants to privilege: Endsley's tidy 3-level SA enum reads as effectively closed, but once team-SA, sensemaking, and common-ground are admitted, the space becomes open/free-form (no single agreed master enumeration unifies cognitive-engineering SA, organizational sensemaking, and HCI common-ground). A decision on scope (single-agent perception-stack vs. distributed/social awareness) would let me commit to 'closed' (Endsley 3-level) vs. 'open'. Also useful: whether the catalog treats 'gestalt' as a capability level (Endsley tiers) or as a style/mode of attention (which would point to different literatures, e.g., attention/framing theory).

values.name: Level 1 — Perception of elements
values.reference: Endsley (1995), "Toward a Theory of Situation Awareness in Dynamic Systems," Human Factors
values.justification: Canonical first level of Endsley's three-level SA model: perceiving the status, attributes, and dynamics of relevant elements in the environment.

values.name: Level 2 — Comprehension of current situation
values.reference: Endsley (1995), three-level SA model
values.justification: Canonical second level: synthesizing Level-1 elements into a holistic understanding of significance relative to goals.

values.name: Level 3 — Projection of future status
values.reference: Endsley (1995), three-level SA model
values.justification: Canonical third level: projecting the future states of elements forward in time — the highest, most demanding tier of SA.

values.name: Shared / team situation awareness
values.reference: Salas et al. (1995); Endsley & Jones shared-SA model
values.justification: Recognized extension to multi-agent settings: the degree to which team members share a common picture on SA requirements (directly relevant to multi-agent AI).

values.name: Distributed situation awareness
values.reference: Stanton et al. (2006), "Distributed situation awareness in dynamic systems," Ergonomics
values.justification: Established systems-level alternative framing: SA as a property held by the socio-technical system (human + artifacts), not only in individual heads — the dominant framing for human-automation joint cognition.

values.name: Sensemaking
values.reference: Klein, Moon & Hoffman (2006), "Making Sense of Sensemaking," IEEE Intelligent Systems; Weick (1995)
values.justification: Naturalistic-decision-making counterpart: the active, iterative process of constructing and revising a frame/mental model — emphasizes the dynamic construction of the whole rather than its momentary state.

B.evidenceNeeded: Confirmation of how the catalog scopes "gestalt": if it means the LEVELS/depth of awareness, Endsley's three-level model is a clean closed backbone (confidence rises toward closed). If it means the TYPE of awareness-construction paradigm (individual SA vs. distributed SA vs. sensemaking vs. ecological/Gibsonian affordance perception), the space is open/hybrid. Cross-checking against the agent-architecture literature (e.g., BDI belief revision, world-model/perception modules in cognitive architectures like Soar/ACT-R, and recent LLM-agent \"context/state estimation\" work) would clarify whether a different field-standard enum should be the backbone instead of Endsley.

values.name: Recognition heuristic
values.reference: Goldstein & Gigerenzer (2002), Psychological Review; Gigerenzer & Todd, Simple Heuristics That Make Us Smart (1999)
values.justification: The paradigmatic fast-and-frugal heuristic: if one of two objects is recognized and the other is not, infer the recognized one scores higher — a canonical, repeatedly studied member of the adaptive toolbox.

values.name: Take-the-best (one-reason decision making)
values.reference: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1996), Psychological Review
values.justification: Cue-ordered lexicographic heuristic (search by validity, stop at first discriminating cue, decide on it); the flagship one-reason heuristic and a fixed reference point in the literature.

values.name: Tallying / unit-weight (equal-weight) model
values.reference: Dawes (1979), 'The robust beauty of improper linear models'; Gigerenzer's toolbox
values.justification: Count cues in favor vs. against with equal weights — the canonical compensatory frugal heuristic contrasted with take-the-best, robust under uncertainty.

values.name: Availability heuristic
values.reference: Tversky & Kahneman (1973, 1974), Cognitive Psychology / Science
values.justification: Judge frequency/probability by ease of retrieval — a foundational, universally cited member of the heuristics-and-biases canon.

values.name: Representativeness heuristic
values.reference: Kahneman & Tversky (1972); Tversky & Kahneman (1974)
values.justification: Judge by similarity to a prototype/category — co-foundational with availability in the classic heuristics-and-biases triad.

values.name: Anchoring-and-adjustment
values.reference: Tversky & Kahneman (1974), Science
values.justification: Start from a salient anchor and adjust insufficiently — the third pillar of the original heuristics-and-biases program, ubiquitously referenced.

values.name: Satisficing (aspiration-level stopping)
values.reference: Simon (1956), Psychological Review; bounded rationality
values.justification: Search until an option meets an aspiration threshold, then stop — the historical root of frugal decision rules and the origin of bounded rationality.

A.evidenceNeeded: A meta-review or handbook (e.g., the Routledge/SAGE handbooks on heuristics, or Gigerenzer & Gaissmaier 2011 Annual Review of Psychology 'Heuristic Decision Making') that either presents a closed master list or explicitly affirms the toolbox is open/recombinant. Also: confirmation that the AI-agent design literature (vs. pure cognitive science) has adopted any subset as a standard configuration enum, which would shift the classification toward a more defined backbone. The decisive point is whether any authority claims completeness; current evidence shows named members exist but the set is explicitly extensible (building-block recombination of search/stop/decision rules), supporting 'hybrid' over 'closed'.

values.name: Availability heuristic
values.reference: Tversky & Kahneman, 'Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases' (Science, 1974)
values.justification: Founding member of the heuristics-and-biases program; judging frequency/probability by ease of recall — a canonical, named rule-of-thumb.

values.name: Representativeness heuristic
values.reference: Tversky & Kahneman (1974); Kahneman & Tversky (1972)
values.justification: Core H&B heuristic: judging category membership by similarity to a prototype; one of the original triad.

values.name: Anchoring-and-adjustment
values.reference: Tversky & Kahneman (1974)
values.justification: Third of the founding triad; estimates formed by adjusting from a salient starting value. Stable, widely cited term.

values.name: Recognition heuristic
values.reference: Goldstein & Gigerenzer, 'Models of ecological rationality' (Psychological Review, 2002); Gigerenzer's 'fast and frugal heuristics' / adaptive toolbox (ABC Research Group, 'Simple Heuristics That Make Us Smart', 1999)
values.justification: Canonical member of the fast-and-frugal toolbox — directly matches 'fast, frugal decisions' — infer the higher value from the recognized option.

values.name: Take-the-best (one-reason decision making)
values.reference: Gigerenzer & Goldstein, 'Reasoning the fast and frugal way' (Psychological Review, 1996)
values.justification: Defining heuristic of the adaptive toolbox; lexicographic cue search stopping at the first discriminating cue.

values.name: Satisficing
values.reference: Herbert Simon, 'Rational choice and the structure of the environment' (Psychological Review, 1956); bounded rationality
values.justification: Original bounded-rationality stopping rule (accept first option above an aspiration level) — the historical root of agent rules-of-thumb.

values.name: Affect heuristic
values.reference: Slovic, Finucane, Peters & MacGregor (2002, 2007)
values.justification: Widely recognized H&B extension: decisions driven by the felt good/bad of the stimulus.

values.name: Elimination by aspects
values.reference: Tversky, 'Elimination by aspects: A theory of choice' (Psychological Review, 1972)
values.justification: Canonical named choice heuristic; sequentially eliminate options failing on attributes in order of importance.

B.evidenceNeeded: The classification turns on scope. Within cognitive science/decision theory there are two well-established, partially-overlapping backbones — the heuristics-and-biases program (Tversky & Kahneman) and the fast-and-frugal/adaptive-toolbox program (Gigerenzer/ABC) — each enumerating named heuristics, plus Simon's bounded rationality as the root. That gives a recognized backbone (hence 'hybrid', not 'open'). But there is no single closed, agreed-upon master enumeration: the two programs disagree on framing (biases-as-errors vs. ecological rationality), and the set of named heuristics keeps growing (fluency, fluency/familiarity, tit-for-tat, default heuristic, 1/N, gaze heuristic). Confidence would rise with: (1) a citation establishing whether the AI-agent-architecture literature has adopted any one of these taxonomies as canonical for agent design (vs. ad hoc 'rules of thumb'); (2) confirmation of whether 'heuristics' here means human-cognition-derived decision rules or engineering heuristics (e.g., admissible search heuristics in A*, planning heuristics), which would point to an entirely different and largely open taxonomy; (3) a recent (post-2015) review consolidating the adaptive toolbox into a fixed list.

values.name: SOLID principles
values.reference: Robert C. Martin (Uncle Bob), 'Design Principles and Design Patterns' (2000); Agile Software Development (2002)
values.justification: The most widely cited closed set of object-oriented design directives (SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, DIP); a canonical, finite, named backbone family for 'how to build'.

values.name: DRY / KISS / YAGNI
values.reference: Hunt & Thomas, 'The Pragmatic Programmer' (1999); Extreme Programming (Beck) for YAGNI
values.justification: The canonical pragmatic operating heuristics — recurring named directives that almost every engineering instruction set references.

values.name: The Twelve-Factor App
values.reference: Adam Wiggins / Heroku, 12factor.net (2011)
values.justification: A recognized enumerated (12-member) doctrine for building/operating software-as-a-service; a canonical finite directive set for delivery.

values.name: Test-Driven Development (red-green-refactor)
values.reference: Kent Beck, 'Test-Driven Development: By Example' (2002)
values.justification: A canonical named workflow directive governing how an agent should sequence building and verification.

values.name: Coding standards / style guides
values.reference: e.g. Google Style Guides; PEP 8 (van Rossum et al.); Airbnb JS Style Guide
values.justification: The open-extension surface: project-specific authored conventions that are inherently free-form yet are the dominant real content of instruction blocks.

values.name: Conway's Law / Separation of Concerns
values.reference: Melvin Conway (1968); Dijkstra, 'On the role of scientific thought' (1974) for SoC
values.justification: Foundational named structural principles routinely encoded as build directives about modularity and ownership.

A.evidenceNeeded: A survey of published agent/system-prompt instruction blocks (e.g., Claude/Cursor/Copilot system prompts, AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md corpora) coded against software-engineering principle taxonomies, to confirm there is no single closed enum and to quantify how dominant the free-form authored portion is versus the recurring named backbone families.

values.name: DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself)
values.reference: Hunt & Thomas, The Pragmatic Programmer (1999)
