values.justification: One of the most widely cited engineering directives; an exemplar of a single operating rule an agent can be told to uphold.

values.name: KISS / YAGNI (simplicity; build only what is needed)
values.reference: Extreme Programming (Beck, 1999) / Unix philosophy lineage
values.justification: Canonical minimalism directives that recur across agent system prompts as 'prefer the simplest change'.

values.name: SOLID principles
values.reference: Robert C. Martin, Agile Software Development (2002)
values.justification: The best-known finite set of OO design directives — but it is one school among many, not THE enum, illustrating the open shape.

values.name: Unix philosophy (do one thing well; compose small tools)
values.reference: McIlroy / Raymond, The Art of Unix Programming (2003)
values.justification: A durable directive-set frequently encoded as agent operating principles for tool design and composition.

values.name: Convention over configuration / follow existing patterns
values.reference: Rails doctrine (DHH); reiterated in LLM agent prompting best-practice (Anthropic agent guidance)
values.justification: A heavily used agent directive ('match the surrounding code style') with real provenance in framework doctrine.

values.name: Test-first / verify-before-claiming-done
values.reference: TDD (Beck, Test-Driven Development, 2002); agent ReAct/reflexion verification practice
values.justification: A recurring operating principle in agent instructions tying action to empirical verification.

B.evidenceNeeded: A widely adopted standard that fixes a FINITE, named set of agent operating directives (e.g., an ISO/IEEE engineering-principles standard, or a dominant LLM-agent prompting spec) would push this toward hybrid/closed. Absent that, surveys of agent system prompts and engineering-principle catalogs confirm the open, multi-school nature.

values.name: Sensory / working memory (short-term context buffer)
values.reference: Atkinson & Shiffrin (1968) multi-store model; Baddeley & Hitch (1974) working memory; mapped to the LLM context window in agent surveys (Wang et al. 2024, 'A Survey on Large Language Model based Autonomous Agents')
values.justification: The canonical transient store: the in-context scratchpad / window holding the current task's active information before it is consolidated or discarded.

values.name: Episodic memory
values.reference: Tulving (1972, 1983) declarative memory split (episodic vs. semantic); carried into agent memory taxonomies (Park et al. 2023 'Generative Agents'; Zhang et al. 2024 'A Survey on the Memory Mechanism of LLM-based Agents')
values.justification: Time-indexed record of specific experienced events ('what happened when') — the standard backbone member for an agent's autobiographical/event log.

values.name: Semantic memory
values.reference: Tulving (1972) declarative memory; standard in agent memory surveys and RAG knowledge-store framing
values.justification: Decontextualized facts, concepts, and world/domain knowledge abstracted away from any single episode — the durable knowledge base.

values.name: Procedural memory
values.reference: Squire (1992) declarative vs. non-declarative (procedural) memory taxonomy; ACT-R declarative/procedural distinction (Anderson 1996); adopted in agent skill-library work (Voyager, Wang et al. 2023)
values.justification: Skills, routines, and learned how-to procedures retrieved as executable competence rather than recalled as facts — the canonical non-declarative member.

values.name: Long-term external store (parametric vs. non-parametric)
values.reference: Lewis et al. (2020) 'Retrieval-Augmented Generation'; agent-memory surveys distinguishing in-weights (parametric) from retrievable external (non-parametric) memory
values.justification: The recognized axis separating knowledge baked into model weights from knowledge held in an external retrievable store (vector DB, files), governing how recall is implemented.

A.evidenceNeeded: A single authoritative, widely-cited LLM-agent memory taxonomy that all surveys converge on (rather than each survey reusing the cognitive-science backbone with idiosyncratic extensions) would let me call this 'closed'. The cognitive-science backbone (sensory/working, episodic/semantic, declarative/procedural) is canonical and finite, but the engineering layer (vector stores, parametric vs. non-parametric, memory streams, reflection/consolidation buffers) is still being extended freely — hence 'hybrid'. Convergence in recent survey literature (e.g., Zhang et al. 2024; Wang et al. 2024) on a fixed enum would settle it.

values.name: Sensory / perceptual buffer memory
values.reference: Atkinson & Shiffrin (1968) modal model of memory; modern variants in cognitive architectures (Soar, ACT-R)
values.justification: The shortest-lived store holding raw perceptual input before encoding; canonical first stage of the standard memory taxonomy that agent designs inherit as the input/observation buffer.

values.name: Short-term / working memory
values.reference: Baddeley & Hitch (1974) working-memory model; Atkinson-Shiffrin STM; agent analog = the in-context window / scratchpad
values.justification: The active, capacity-limited store the agent reasons over in the moment; in LLM agents this is the prompt context, universally recognized as the working-memory tier.

values.name: Long-term memory (umbrella)
values.reference: Atkinson & Shiffrin (1968); Tulving (1972)
values.justification: The durable store partitioned into the declarative/non-declarative subtypes below; the canonical backbone every agent-memory survey (e.g., Generative Agents, MemGPT, A-MEM) maps onto.

values.name: Episodic memory
values.reference: Tulving (1972, 1983) — episodic vs. semantic distinction; Park et al. (2023) Generative Agents 'memory stream'
values.justification: Time-indexed records of specific experienced events; the canonical declarative subtype and the dominant model for agent event logs / memory streams.

values.name: Semantic memory
values.reference: Tulving (1972); knowledge-graph / vector-store agent memory (RAG, A-MEM)
values.justification: Decontextualized facts, concepts, and general knowledge abstracted from episodes; the second canonical declarative subtype and the basis of knowledge-base agent memory.

values.name: Procedural memory
values.reference: Squire (1992) declarative vs. non-declarative taxonomy; Anderson ACT-R procedural module
values.justification: Non-declarative memory for skills/how-to (production rules, learned policies); canonical non-declarative subtype, realized in agents as tools/skills/cached procedures.

values.name: Profile / persona memory
values.reference: Mei et al. (2024) 'A Survey on the Memory Mechanism of LLM-based Agents'; commercial systems (ChatGPT memory, MemGPT persistent persona)
values.justification: Persistent self/user attributes and preferences; a recognized first-class store in agent-memory surveys distinct from generic semantic memory, the field-standard extension beyond the cognitive backbone.

B.evidenceNeeded: A systematic LLM-agent memory survey (e.g., Mei et al. 2024; Zhang et al. 'Survey on Memory in LLM Agents') to confirm whether the field has converged on a closed enum (sensory/short-term/long-term {episodic, semantic, procedural} + profile) or treats memory types as an open, system-specific design choice; plus a sample of production agent frameworks (MemGPT, LangChain/LangMem, A-MEM, Letta) to count how often novel store types appear beyond the cognitive-science backbone.

values.name: Responsibility / accountability assignment (RACI)
values.reference: RACI matrix (project/organizational management; PMI BoK lineage)
values.justification: The canonical decomposition of a remit: who is Responsible vs Accountable vs Consulted vs Informed — the field-standard backbone for stating what a role owns.

values.name: In-scope / out-of-scope boundary
values.reference: Requirements engineering & project scope management (BABOK, PMBOK scope statement)
values.justification: The defining structure of a mandate is the explicit inclusion/exclusion boundary; 'what is out of scope' is a first-class, standardized scope-statement element.

values.name: Goal / objective (terminal mandate)
values.reference: Goal-oriented agent design; BDI architecture (Rao & Georgeff); GORE / i* goal modeling
values.justification: A mandate is canonically expressed as the goal-state the agent is charged to bring about — the 'desire' layer in belief-desire-intention agents.

values.name: Task / function remit
values.reference: Task-oriented dialogue & agent taxonomies; functional role specification in multi-agent systems (FIPA, AGR/Gaia role model)
values.justification: Roles in MAS methodologies (Gaia, AGR) are defined by the set of tasks/services a role is obligated to perform — the operational granularity of a mandate.

values.name: Authority / permission boundary (scope of action)
values.reference: AI safety & access control; principle of least privilege; capability/authority limits in autonomous-agent governance
values.justification: A mandate includes what the agent is permitted to act on; least-privilege scoping is the recognized safety-side framing of remit limits.

values.name: Priority/obligation weighting (MoSCoW)
values.reference: MoSCoW prioritization (DSDM / requirements management)
values.justification: Within a remit, Must/Should/Could/Won't distinguishes core obligations from optional and explicitly-excluded duties — a standard way to grade a mandate's contents.

A.evidenceNeeded: A survey of agent-specification frameworks (e.g., AutoGPT/LangChain agent 'role' fields, CrewAI 'role/goal/backstory', FIPA/Gaia role models, agent-card/spec standards) to confirm whether the field converges on a single named schema for 'mandate' versus borrowing ad hoc from RACI/scope-statement traditions. Also whether AI-safety literature has crystallized a standard 'authority boundary' vocabulary distinct from generic least-privilege.

values.name: Scope of authority / charter (responsibilities + boundaries)
values.reference: Organizational role theory & RACI charters (Katz & Kahn, The Social Psychology of Organizations, 1966; PMI RACI responsibility-assignment matrix)
values.justification: The canonical way a remit is specified across management science is a free-text charter naming what the role owns and its boundaries — there is no closed set of charters, illustrating the dimension's open shape.

values.name: Goal / task specification
values.reference: BDI agent architecture (Rao & Georgeff, 1995) and goal-oriented agent design; system-prompt 'objective' fields in LLM agent guidance (OpenAI/Anthropic agent building guides)
values.justification: In agent architecture the mandate is given as a goal or task description supplied per-deployment, not chosen from an enumerated catalog — exemplar of free-form remit.

values.name: Job design / scope-of-work
values.reference: Job Characteristics Model (Hackman & Oldham, 1976); job-description scope-of-work practice
values.justification: Remit is operationalized as task identity and significance defined ad hoc for each office; the space of jobs is generative, not enumerable.

values.name: In-scope vs out-of-scope (guardrails / refusal boundary)
values.reference: Responsible-AI policy specs and tool/agent 'allowed actions' scoping (NIST AI RMF; Anthropic/OpenAI safety guardrail patterns)
values.justification: Modern agents declare explicit out-of-scope clauses and escalation triggers, but the content of those clauses is bespoke per agent — structural pattern, open content.

values.name: Span of control / jurisdiction
values.reference: Classical administrative theory (Gulick & Urwick, Papers on the Science of Administration, 1937; Fayol)
values.justification: A remit is bounded by a jurisdiction (which subjects/resources the office may act on); jurisdictions are domain-defined and unbounded, confirming the dimension is open.

values.name: Decision rights / accountability boundary
values.reference: Decision-rights frameworks (RAPID, Bain & Company; agency theory, Jensen & Meckling, 1976)
values.justification: Mandate includes which decisions the agent may make versus must defer; this is configured per role from an open domain rather than drawn from a fixed taxonomy.

B.evidenceNeeded: A recognized, finite taxonomy of agent remits/offices (analogous to how Sheridan-Verplank enumerates automation levels) would shift this toward hybrid/closed. Useful evidence: a standards body (NIST, ISO/IEC JTC1 SC42), a widely-cited multi-agent role catalog, or an HCI 'function allocation' taxonomy that enumerates remit *content* (not just authority degree or function stage). Absent such an enumeration, the field treats mandate as a free-text charter, supporting 'open'. Note the adjacent dimensions (autonomy/authority level, function stage) ARE closed (Parasuraman-Sheridan-Wickens 2000), so care is needed not to conflate remit content with authority degree."

values.name: User/operator message (natural-language utterance)
values.reference: Conversational/dialogue agent architectures; speech-act theory (Searle 1969); ReAct (Yao et al. 2022) treats the task instruction as the opening observation
values.justification: The default percept for chat-shaped agents: a parsed human utterance is the single input that opens the turn — the canonical backbone case.

values.name: Tool/action result (observation o_t)
values.reference: ReAct (Yao et al. 2022); MDP/POMDP formalism where the agent reads observation o_t after action a_{t-1}; Function-calling / tool-use loops (Toolformer, OpenAI/Anthropic tool APIs)
values.justification: In the sense-act loop the returned tool output is the canonical observation that opens the next reasoning step — the formal POMDP 'observation' element.

values.name: Environment/world percept (sensory state)
values.reference: Russell & Norvig, AIMA — agent = function from percept sequences to actions; the 'percept' is the agent's perceptual input from the environment
values.justification: AIMA's foundational definition makes the environment percept the prototypical input opening each agent cycle; canonical in the textbook taxonomy.

values.name: Event / signal (trigger)
values.reference: Event-driven architectures; BDI agent 'events' (Rao & Georgeff 1995) that trigger plan selection; webhook/callback-driven agents
values.justification: A discrete event or interrupt is a recognized percept type that opens a turn in reactive/event-driven and BDI agents.

values.name: Scheduled / timer tick (self-initiated wake)
values.reference: Cron/heartbeat agents; autonomous-loop architectures (AutoGPT-style self-continuation); the 'no-input' continuation observation
values.justification: A timer or empty continuation prompt is a real percept form for proactive agents — the turn opens with elapsed-time rather than external content.

values.name: Inter-agent message (ACL/A2A)
values.reference: FIPA-ACL agent communication language; speech-act-based multi-agent messaging; A2A / multi-agent orchestration protocols
values.justification: In multi-agent systems the opening input is a structured message from a peer agent, a standardized percept category in MAS literature.

A.evidenceNeeded: A single authoritative taxonomy that enumerates *percept forms* as a closed set would settle open-vs-closed. AIMA defines 'percept' but does not enumerate a finite typology of percept kinds; POMDP formalism makes 'observation' a free typed variable, not an enum. Confirmation would come from (a) a recognized HCI/agent-IO taxonomy of input/trigger types, or (b) a standard like FIPA performatives if the dimension is scoped to message percepts only. The field treats the *channel/source* as having a loose recognized backbone (user / tool-result / environment / event / timer / peer-agent) but the percept *content form* is inherently open (any parseable payload), which is why I classify hybrid rather than closed.

values.name: Percept (atomic input at time t)
values.reference: Russell & Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach (AIMA), agent model: f: P* → A maps percept sequences to actions
values.justification: The field's foundational term for exactly this dimension — the single observation the agent reads at the top of one act; defines the slot itself, not its content type.

values.name: Observation (POMDP/RL sense)
values.reference: Partially Observable Markov Decision Process formalism; OpenAI Gym/Gymnasium step() returns an observation
values.justification: Canonical RL/control term for the per-step input; in POMDPs the observation o ∈ Ω is explicitly the parsed window onto hidden state that opens each decision step.

values.name: User / human message (instruction turn)
values.reference: OpenAI/Anthropic chat-completions message roles; ReAct (Yao et al. 2022) prompt-driven turns
values.justification: In LLM agents the most common turn-opener is a natural-language request — the dominant percept form for conversational/instruction-following agents.

values.name: Tool / function result (observation step)
values.reference: ReAct's Thought→Action→Observation loop; OpenAI tool-calling 'tool' role; MCP tool results
values.justification: The canonical machine-generated percept: a turn opened by the returned result of a prior action, the 'Observation' in the ReAct cycle.

values.name: Environment / sensor event (sensory input)
values.reference: AIMA agent taxonomy (sensors→percepts); robotics/embodied-agent perception pipelines
values.justification: For embodied or event-driven agents the turn opener is a sensor/event reading (vision frame, state delta, webhook), the classic 'percept from sensors'.

values.name: System / scheduler trigger (autonomous wake)
values.reference: BDI agent architectures (Rao & Georgeff) event queue; cron/daemon agent loops; autonomous-agent wake events
values.justification: A turn can open with no external content — a timer/scheduler/internal-goal event — recognized in proactive/BDI agents as a percept-equivalent trigger.

B.evidenceNeeded: A standards-grade source that explicitly enumerates a CLOSED set of turn-opener types for LLM agents (e.g., a fixed message-role taxonomy treated as exhaustive). The classification is 'hybrid' because AIMA/POMDP supply a strong canonical backbone term ('percept'/'observation') and the LLM message-role + ReAct vocabulary supplies a recognized small set of concrete forms (user message, tool result, system trigger, sensor event), but no field declares the content-types of percepts to be a finite exhaustive enum — new modalities/event sources extend it freely. Confirmation that practitioners treat the message-role/observation-source list as a backbone-plus-extensions rather than a fixed enum would settle hybrid vs. open.

values.name: The 12 Brand Archetypes (Innocent, Sage, Explorer, Outlaw/Rebel, Magician, Hero, Lover, Jester, Everyman/Regular Guy, Caregiver, Ruler, Creator)
values.reference: Mark & Pearson, The Hero and the Outlaw (2001), operationalizing Jungian archetypes for brand/character design
values.justification: The single most widely-adopted finite taxonomy of projected character in branding and conversational-agent persona design; treated as a canonical enumerable backbone.

values.name: Jungian archetypes (Self, Shadow, Anima/Animus, Persona, plus the archetypal figures: Hero, Mother, Trickster, Wise Old Man, etc.)
values.reference: C.G. Jung, The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW Vol. 9)
values.justification: The psychological provenance underneath nearly all character/persona enumerations; the term 'persona' itself is Jungian.

values.name: Stock dramatic character archetypes (Hero, Mentor, Threshold Guardian, Herald, Shapeshifter, Shadow, Trickster, Ally)
values.reference: Vogler, The Writer's Journey (adapting Campbell's monomyth)
values.justification: A recognized finite cast used in narrative/character design and frequently borrowed for designing conversational-agent personalities.

values.name: OCEAN / Big Five personality dimensions (Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism)
values.reference: Costa & McCrae (1992); applied to agents via 'personality of conversational agents' HCI literature
values.justification: The field-standard *parametric* (rather than enumerated) representation of personality, showing persona is also realized as a continuous trait space, not just discrete labels.

values.name: Designed UX/voice personas (e.g., Alexa, Siri, Clippy, Cortana — bespoke named characters)
values.reference: Nass & Brave, Wired for Speech (2005); CASA/Media Equation paradigm; product persona/voice-design practice
values.justification: Demonstrates the open tail: production agent personas are authored ad hoc (tone, register, named character) rather than drawn from any fixed list.

A.evidenceNeeded: Evidence that any single taxonomy is treated as authoritative across AI-agent design specifically (rather than borrowed from branding/narrative): e.g., a standards body or widely-cited agent-persona framework that fixes an enumeration. Conversely, a corpus survey of deployed assistant personas showing they predominantly use free-form authored characters would push toward 'open'. The classification is 'hybrid' precisely because a recognized backbone (12 archetypes / Jungian / Big Five) coexists with unbounded bespoke persona authoring.

values.name: The Innocent
values.reference: Jungian archetypes via Mark & Pearson, 'The Hero and the Outlaw' (2001) — brand archetype canon
values.justification: One of the 12 brand archetypes, the dominant marketing/brand taxonomy used to assign a character; rooted in Jungian archetype theory.

values.name: The Sage
values.reference: Mark & Pearson 12 brand archetypes (Jung)
values.justification: Canonical 'knowledge/truth' archetype frequently mapped onto expert/advisor agent personas.

values.name: The Hero
values.reference: Mark & Pearson 12 brand archetypes; Campbell monomyth lineage
values.justification: Core archetype with strong provenance in both brand theory and narratology, widely used to characterize agent voice.

values.name: The Caregiver
values.reference: Mark & Pearson 12 brand archetypes
values.justification: Canonical nurturing/service archetype — the prototypical assistant persona in HCI/conversational-agent design.

values.name: The Jester
values.reference: Mark & Pearson 12 brand archetypes
values.justification: Canonical playful/humorous archetype, a recognized member of the closed 12-set backbone.

values.name: The Magician / The Creator / The Ruler / The Explorer / The Lover / The Outlaw / The Everyman
values.reference: Mark & Pearson 12 brand archetypes (remaining members of the 12)
values.justification: Completes the 12-archetype backbone — the most-cited finite taxonomy for projected character.

values.name: Big Five trait profile (e.g., high Agreeableness / high Openness)
values.reference: Costa & McCrae Five-Factor Model (OCEAN); applied to agents in 'Personality Traits in Large Language Models' (Serapio-García et al., 2023)
values.justification: The dominant psychometric backbone for parameterizing persona as continuous trait dimensions rather than discrete archetypes — shows the dimension is also expressible as open continuous values.

B.evidenceNeeded: Confirmation of which framing the cataloging effort treats as authoritative for 'persona': the discrete archetype backbone (Jung/Mark-Pearson 12) vs. continuous trait psychometrics (Big Five/HEXACO) vs. role-label conventions in conversational-AI design (e.g., persona-chat datasets). Evidence that no single closed enum is treated as exhaustive in the AI-agent literature (persona is routinely free-text system-prompt specification) would confirm the 'hybrid' classification: a recognized archetype backbone with unbounded free extension.

values.name: Base model / foundation model identity
values.reference: Model cards (Mitchell et al., 2019, FAccT) and the foundation-model framing (Bommasani et al., Stanford CRFM, 2021)
values.justification: The most basic provenance fact for any LLM agent is which pretrained base it descends from (e.g. a named foundation model + version); model cards canonicalize recording this lineage.

values.name: Fine-tune / adaptation lineage (parent checkpoint)
values.reference: Transfer-learning and PEFT literature (Howard & Ruder ULMFiT 2018; Hu et al. LoRA 2021); Hugging Face Hub 'base_model' / 'finetuned_from' metadata convention
values.justification: An agent often descends from a parent checkpoint via fine-tuning/LoRA/distillation; the parent-pointer is a recognized, recorded provenance link forming a derivation chain.

values.name: Training-data provenance / dataset lineage
values.reference: Datasheets for Datasets (Gebru et al., 2018) and Data Provenance Initiative (Longpre et al., 2023)
values.justification: Lineage of what corpora the agent was trained on is a standardized provenance axis in responsible-ML documentation, distinct from model-weight ancestry.

values.name: Template / archetype-instance derivation
values.reference: Software design-pattern lineage (prototype/clone patterns, GoF 1994) and class-instance inheritance in OOP
values.justification: At the configuration level an agent can be marked as derived-from a template, persona archetype, or another agent definition (a 'forked from' / 'instance-of' relation), the engineering sense of descent.

values.name: W3C PROV provenance record (wasDerivedFrom)
values.reference: W3C PROV-DM / PROV-O Recommendation (2013)
values.justification: The interoperable standard for expressing 'what an entity was derived from' (wasDerivedFrom, wasGeneratedBy, wasAttributedTo) — the generic, domain-agnostic schema any agent-lineage claim can be encoded in.

values.name: Authorship / vendor & creator attribution
values.reference: Model cards 'developed by' field; SPDX / supply-chain provenance (SLSA framework, OpenSSF)
values.justification: Origin marking includes who/what organization produced the agent — a recognized supply-chain provenance attribute (creator, publisher, build origin).

A.evidenceNeeded: Whether any single field has standardized a FINITE enumerable vocabulary specifically for 'provenance type' (rather than free-form derivation graphs). W3C PROV, model cards, and the Data Provenance Initiative all treat provenance as relations over arbitrary entities (open/graph-structured), not as a closed enum — so closing this would require a recognized taxonomy that fixes a fixed list of lineage-kinds. Surveying agent-framework metadata schemas (e.g. agent cards, MCP, model registries) for a constrained lineage enum would confirm or refute the 'open' classification.

values.name: Base/foundation model lineage (derived-from)
values.reference: Model Cards (Mitchell et al., 2019); Hugging Face base_model / model-index metadata; Llama/Mistral derivative-naming conventions
values.justification: The dominant real-world provenance marking for agents: which foundation model (and fine-tune chain) the agent descends from — a free-form pointer, not a closed enum.

values.name: Training-data provenance
values.reference: W3C PROV-O (prov:wasDerivedFrom / prov:wasGeneratedBy, 2013); Datasheets for Datasets (Gebru et al., 2018); Data Provenance Initiative (2023)
values.justification: Standard lineage axis recording which corpora/sources the agent's behavior descends from; PROV gives a vocabulary but the value space (datasets) is unbounded.

values.name: Software supply-chain provenance
values.reference: SLSA framework (provenance attestations); in-toto; CycloneDX/SPDX SBOM (NTIA)
values.justification: Engineering-standard origin marking of the build artifact and its dependency lineage — canonical practice for 'what this descends from' at the package level, but values are arbitrary identifiers.

values.name: Forked/templated agent ancestry (parent agent or template)
values.reference: Git/VCS lineage (commit ancestry, fork graph); agent-framework templates (e.g. archetype/base-agent inheritance)
values.justification: Agents are commonly instantiated by cloning a parent or template; the 'descends-from' link is a free pointer into a DAG, illustrating the open shape.

values.name: Archetypal descent (brand/character lineage)
values.reference: Jung's archetypes via Mark & Pearson, 'The Hero and the Outlaw' (2001) brand-archetype framework
values.justification: For persona/brand-shaped agents, provenance can mark descent from an archetype family — a recognized typology, but used here as one open source among many, not a closed enum for provenance itself.

values.name: Authorship/origin attribution (creator, organization, license)
values.reference: W3C PROV (prov:wasAttributedTo / prov:Agent); Creative Commons & SPDX license identifiers; model-card 'Developed by'
values.justification: The 'who made it / under what terms' facet of lineage; standardized attribution vocabularies exist but the attributed entities are an open set.

B.evidenceNeeded: A single authoritative taxonomy that enumerates a finite, named set of provenance *kinds* for agents (rather than vocabularies like PROV/SLSA that supply relations but leave the value space open). If such an enum existed in MLOps governance or an agent-architecture standard, this would shift toward hybrid; absent that, the open classification holds. Also helpful: evidence of whether the question intends provenance as discrete categorical *modes* (e.g., scratch-built vs. fine-tuned vs. forked vs. archetype-descended) versus free-form lineage pointers — the former could support a hybrid backbone.

values.name: Field (subject-matter / domain register)
values.reference: Halliday's register theory — the three register variables (field, tenor, mode), Systemic Functional Linguistics (Halliday & Hasan 1985, Language, Context, and Text)
values.justification: Field is one of the three canonical context-of-situation variables governing how language varies by what is being talked about (technical vs. lay vocabulary, domain specificity).

values.name: Tenor (relationship / formality between participants)
values.reference: Halliday's register theory (field/tenor/mode); SFL
values.justification: Tenor is the canonical variable capturing the social relationship and formality/power/solidarity between speaker and addressee — the core of audience-relative tuning.

values.name: Mode (channel / textual organization)
values.reference: Halliday's register theory (field/tenor/mode); SFL
values.justification: Mode is the canonical variable for the role language plays (spoken vs. written, planned vs. spontaneous, channel constraints) — load-bearing for medium-specific fit.

values.name: Formality continuum (frozen / formal / consultative / casual / intimate)
values.reference: Martin Joos, The Five Clocks (1961) — the five 'styles' of English
values.justification: Joos's five registers are the most widely cited closed enumeration of formality levels, a recognized backbone for register-as-formality.

values.name: Audience design / recipient design
values.reference: Allan Bell, 'Language Style as Audience Design' (Language in Society, 1984); Sacks/Schegloff recipient design in CA
values.justification: Names the mechanism by which a speaker tunes style to the present addressee/auditors/overhearers — the in-the-moment audience-relative half of the dimension.

values.name: Accommodation (convergence / divergence)
values.reference: Communication Accommodation Theory — Giles et al. (Howard Giles, 1973 onward)
values.justification: CAT supplies the canonical moves (converge toward, diverge from, maintain relative to the interlocutor) — the dynamic, moment-to-moment adjustment strategies.

A.evidenceNeeded: Whether the field treats register as a fixed enum vs. a parameter space is the crux. Confidence would rise with: (a) a survey establishing whether Halliday's field/tenor/mode is universally accepted as THE backbone vs. competing frameworks (Biber's multidimensional analysis treats register as continuous dimensions derived empirically, which pushes toward 'open'); (b) evidence on how HCI/conversational-AI literature operationalizes register adaptation (style transfer, persona conditioning) — whether they adopt a closed taxonomy or free-form style vectors; (c) clarification of whether 'register-fit' here means the variable set (closed: 3 Hallidayan variables), the formality levels (closed: Joos's 5), or the adaptation strategy (CAT's converge/diverge) — these resolve to different answers.

values.name: Field (subject matter / domain of discourse)
values.reference: Halliday's register theory / Systemic Functional Linguistics (Halliday & Hasan, 1985, 'Language, Context, and Text')
values.justification: One of the three canonical register variables: what the language is about, governing technicality and lexical density — a recognized backbone dimension along which any utterance can be tuned.

values.name: Tenor (relationship / power & solidarity between participants)
values.reference: Halliday's register theory / SFL (Halliday & Hasan, 1985); roots in Brown & Gilman (1960) power/solidarity
values.justification: Second canonical register variable: the social distance, status differential, and affect toward the reader — directly the 'audience' axis of register-fit.

values.name: Mode (channel / textual organization)
values.reference: Halliday's register theory / SFL (Halliday & Hasan, 1985)
values.justification: Third canonical register variable: spoken vs. written, planned vs. spontaneous, role of language — the medium-fit component of register.

values.name: Formality (frozen / formal / consultative / casual / intimate)
values.reference: Martin Joos, 'The Five Clocks' (1961) — the five styles
values.justification: The most widely cited closed scale of stylistic register; an enumerable backbone for the formality slider specifically.

values.name: Audience design / recipient design (addressee, auditor, overhearer, eavesdropper)
values.reference: Allan Bell, 'Language Style as Audience Design' (1984); conversation-analytic 'recipient design' (Sacks, Schegloff & Jefferson, 1974)
values.justification: Canonical model of how speakers shift style by who is in the audience frame — the dynamic 'in the moment' tuning mechanism.

values.name: Accommodation (convergence / divergence / maintenance)
values.reference: Communication Accommodation Theory (Giles et al., 1973 onward)
values.justification: Names the canonical moves an agent makes to adjust toward or away from the reader's style — the operational verbs of register-fit.

B.evidenceNeeded: Whether the AI-agent/HCI literature has converged on a single named scheme for "register adaptation" (it largely borrows sociolinguistics ad hoc). Confirmation of whether to treat this as one slider (formality, Joos's closed 5) or the multi-axis backbone (Halliday's field/tenor/mode), which determines closed-vs-hybrid. Also whether persona/style-control work in NLG (e.g., style-transfer attribute sets) supplies a competing canonical enumeration. The classification is 'hybrid' because the field gives a recognized backbone (the three register variables; Joos's formality scale) but the concrete realizations per audience are open and unbounded.

values.name: Optimizing (maximizing)
values.reference: Simon, H. (1955/1956) bounded rationality; classical statistical decision theory (von Neumann–Morgenstern expected-utility maximization)
values.justification: The canonical baseline: defer commitment until the option with the highest evaluated utility is identified; the normative pole every other commitment style is defined against.

values.name: Satisficing
values.reference: Herbert Simon, 'A Behavioral Model of Rational Choice' (1955) — bounded rationality
values.justification: The single most-cited alternative commitment rule: stop deliberating and commit to the first option that clears an aspiration/'good enough' threshold; a foundational, named member.

values.name: Recognition-Primed Decision (intuitive commitment)
values.reference: Gary Klein, RPD model / Naturalistic Decision Making (1989, 'Sources of Power' 1998)
values.justification: Field-standard account of expert single-option commitment: recognize a situation, mentally simulate one workable course of action, and commit without comparative search.

values.name: Elimination by Aspects (heuristic narrowing)
values.reference: Amos Tversky, 'Elimination by Aspects: A Theory of Choice' (1972)
values.justification: A canonical bounded-rationality commitment strategy: sequentially eliminate options failing salient attributes until one remains; established heuristic-decision member.

values.name: Evidence-accumulation to threshold (drift-diffusion / sequential sampling)
values.reference: Ratcliff diffusion decision model (1978); Wald, Sequential Analysis / SPRT (1947)
values.justification: The dominant process-level model of when commitment happens: accumulate evidence until a decision boundary is crossed; boundary height tunes speed–accuracy / caution, a direct 'how decisively' knob.

values.name: Deferral / option-keeping (reversible, real-options commitment)
values.reference: Real Options theory (Dixit & Pindyck, 1994); status-quo/omission bias (Samuelson & Zeckhauser, 1988)
values.justification: Recognized commitment style of deliberately not committing — keeping choices open under uncertainty to preserve future flexibility; the explicit low-resolve pole.

A.evidenceNeeded: A single authoritative taxonomy that enumerates 'decision-commitment styles' as a closed set under one name would settle this. The field has a strong, well-named BACKBONE (optimizing vs. satisficing vs. recognition-primed vs. heuristic-narrowing vs. threshold-accumulation vs. deferral), but these come from distinct literatures (bounded rationality, NDM, mathematical psychology, real-options) rather than one canonical enum — hence 'hybrid'. Confirmation would come from a decision-science review article or HCI/automation handbook that consolidates these into one labeled dimension of commitment style, or evidence that a specific agent-architecture standard (e.g., BDI 'commitment strategies': blind/single-minded/open-minded commitment, Rao & Georgeff 1991) is the intended frame — which would shift the canonical members toward that 3-way intention-persistence taxonomy.

values.name: Maximizing
values.reference: Simon (1956) bounded rationality; Schwartz et al. (2002), 'Maximizing Versus Satisficing'
values.justification: Canonical decision-commitment style: defer commitment until the best option is identified across the option set — the optimization pole of the classic maximize/satisfice contrast.

values.name: Satisficing
values.reference: Herbert Simon (1956), 'Rational Choice and the Structure of the Environment'
values.justification: The foundational alternative to maximizing: commit to the first option crossing an aspiration threshold — the most cited decision-stopping rule in bounded-rationality theory.

values.name: Take-the-best / fast-and-frugal heuristic
values.reference: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1996); Gigerenzer & Todd, 'Simple Heuristics That Make Us Smart' (1999)
values.justification: A recognized one-reason decision rule: stop deliberation and commit on the first discriminating cue — a distinct, well-provenanced commitment style.

values.name: Vigilant decision-making
values.reference: Janis & Mann (1977), 'Decision Making: A Psychological Analysis of Conflict, Choice, and Commitment'; Mann et al. (1997) Melbourne Decision Making Questionnaire
values.justification: Backbone coping pattern: thorough canvassing then deliberate commitment — the adaptive pole of an empirically validated decision-style instrument.

values.name: Defensive avoidance / Procrastination
values.reference: Janis & Mann (1977) conflict-theory model; Melbourne DMQ subscales
values.justification: Validated maladaptive commitment styles (buck-passing, procrastinating, rationalizing) — the chronic deferral pole opposite vigilance.

values.name: Hypervigilance (panic/impulsive commitment)
values.reference: Janis & Mann (1977); Mann et al. (1997)
values.justification: Premature, time-pressured seizing of an option without full deliberation — the snap-decision pole on the same validated taxonomy.

values.name: Action vs. State orientation
values.reference: Kuhl (1985, 1994), Action Control Theory
values.justification: Dispositional commitment construct: action-oriented individuals readily disengage deliberation and enact a choice; state-oriented ruminate and stall — a measured personality axis of decision-commitment.

B.evidenceNeeded: A single authoritative cross-field taxonomy that explicitly enumerates 'decision-commitment styles' as a closed set would settle whether this is closed rather than hybrid. The literatures (Simon's maximize/satisfice, Gigerenzer's heuristics, Janis-Mann conflict theory, Scott & Bruce's General Decision-Making Style inventory, Kuhl's action/state orientation) each offer partial, well-validated backbones but no field has unified them into one canonical enum; confirmation from a decision-science review consolidating these, or evidence that the General Decision-Making Style (rational/intuitive/dependent/avoidant/spontaneous) instrument is treated as THE standard, would shift the classification.

values.name: Text / language input
values.reference: Russell & Norvig, AIMA (PEAS/percept framework); the dominant modality for LLM agents (GPT-4, Claude). Multimodal taxonomies (e.g. Baltrušaitis et al., 'Multimodal Machine Learning: A Survey', TPAMI 2019) treat language as a core modality.
values.justification: The primary percept channel for current language-model agents; tokenized natural-language and structured text is the canonical default input.

values.name: Visual / image input
values.reference: Computer vision literature; multimodal model surveys (Baltrušaitis 2019); vision-language models (CLIP, GPT-4V, Gemini).
values.justification: Vision is a canonical perceptual modality across cognitive science and ML; image-in is a first-class sensor for VLM agents.

values.name: Audio / speech input
values.reference: Speech recognition (ASR) literature; multimodal surveys; Whisper, audio-LM systems.
values.justification: Hearing/audio is a canonical sensory channel; speech and ambient-sound input is a recognized agent modality.

values.name: Video / spatiotemporal input
values.reference: Video understanding literature; multimodal model surveys (vision+temporal); embodied-AI benchmarks.
values.justification: Time-extended visual perception is treated as its own modality (motion, events) distinct from still images.

values.name: Proprioceptive / embodied & sensorimotor state
values.reference: Robotics and embodied-cognition literature (Brooks subsumption; embodied AI / RL state observations); AIMA agent–environment percept loop.
values.justification: For embodied/robotic agents, internal-body and physical-environment sensors (force, position, depth, lidar) are a canonical perceptual class.

values.name: Structured / digital tool & API observations (incl. GUI/screen state)
values.reference: Tool-use and agent frameworks (ReAct, Yao et al. 2022; Toolformer; computer-use agents); HCI human-automation interaction literature.
values.justification: Software agents perceive via tool returns, file/DB reads, sensor APIs, and screen-scrapes — a recognized 'percept' channel in agent architectures even if not a human sense.

A.evidenceNeeded: A single authoritative, citable taxonomy that fixes the exact membership and granularity of agent input modalities (e.g., whether 'video' is separate from 'image', whether 'sensor/API' counts as a modality). The multimodal-ML surveys give a recognized backbone (text/vision/audio + others) but draw boundaries differently, and embodied-robotics sensor lists are open-ended (any transducer), which is why this is hybrid rather than strictly closed. Cross-referencing AIMA's percept framework, Baltrušaitis et al. (2019), and a current multimodal-foundation-model survey would sharpen both membership and the open/closed call.

values.name: Visual / image input
values.reference: Cognitive science sensory-modality taxonomy (vision); multimodal ML literature (CLIP, GPT-4V, Gemini) — "image" as a standard input modality
values.justification: Human vision is one of the canonical exteroceptive senses, and "image" is the most established non-text input channel for AI agents (vision encoders, VLMs).

values.name: Auditory / audio input
values.reference: Sensory-modality taxonomy (audition); speech/ASR and audio-ML literature (Whisper, audio transformers)
values.justification: Hearing is a canonical sense; audio (speech + non-speech) is a recognized first-class input modality in multimodal agent stacks.

values.name: Textual / linguistic input
values.reference: NLP / HCI; the dominant modality for LLM agents (token streams, prompts, documents)
values.justification: Text is the backbone perceptual channel for language-model agents; though not a biological sense, it is the field-standard primary input modality.

values.name: Tactile / haptic & force input
values.reference: Sensory-modality taxonomy (somatosensation/touch); robotics sensing (force-torque, tactile arrays)
values.justification: Touch/proprioception is a canonical human sense and a standard robot-agent sensor class for contact-rich manipulation.

values.name: Spatial / depth & motion (LiDAR, proprioception, IMU)
values.reference: Robotics & autonomous-systems sensing taxonomy; cognitive science proprioception/vestibular sense
values.justification: Embodied agents canonically perceive geometry and self-motion (depth cameras, LiDAR, encoders, IMUs) — the vestibular/proprioceptive analogue.

values.name: Symbolic / API & environment-state observations
values.reference: RL & agent-architecture literature (the "observation" in the perceive→decide→act loop; gym observation spaces; tool/API returns)
values.justification: For software agents the dominant 'sensor' is structured environment state (API responses, tool outputs, DOM, logs) — the field-standard observation channel beyond biological senses.

B.evidenceNeeded: Whether the catalog intends biological/perceptual modalities (cognitive science: the classic five senses plus proprioception/interoception/vestibular — a closed list) or computational input channels for software/robotic agents (open and ever-growing: any data stream, API, or instrument). The classification hinges on that scoping decision. A canonical multimodal-AI taxonomy paper or a robotics sensor ontology (e.g., a sensor-fusion survey) defining a fixed enumeration would push this toward 'closed'; the de facto practice of agents ingesting arbitrary structured data streams pushes toward 'open' — hence the hybrid call.

values.name: Frontier hosted LLM (proprietary API model)
values.reference: Stanford HELM / HAI AI Index taxonomy of foundation models; provider model catalogs (OpenAI GPT-4/4o/o-series, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini)
values.justification: The dominant agent substrate today is a closed-weights model accessed via a hosted inference API; this is the canonical default class in nearly every agent framework (LangChain, AutoGPT, OpenAI Assistants).

values.name: Open-weights LLM (self-hostable model)
values.reference: Foundation model literature; Meta Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, Falcon model releases; HuggingFace model hub taxonomy
values.justification: A recognized first-class substrate class — models whose weights are downloadable and runnable on owned hardware, the standard alternative to hosted APIs in agent deployment.

values.name: Local inference runtime (on-device / edge serving)
values.reference: Inference-serving ecosystem: Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM, TGI (Text Generation Inference), GGUF format
values.justification: The runtime axis of 'substrate' — where/how the model executes (local vs cloud) is an established configuration distinction orthogonal to which model, recognized across the serving-stack literature.

values.name: Hosted inference platform / model-serving cloud
values.reference: Amazon Bedrock, Azure OpenAI Service, Google Vertex AI, Together/Fireworks/Groq inference providers
values.justification: A canonical runtime substrate: the managed cloud that serves a model behind an endpoint, distinct from the model family itself and routinely specified in agent configs.

values.name: Small / specialized model (SLM, distilled or fine-tuned)
values.reference: SLM literature (e.g., Phi series, Gemma); distillation and PEFT/LoRA fine-tuning research
values.justification: Recognized substrate class for cost/latency-constrained agents — smaller or task-specialized models are a standard configuration choice in multi-agent and routing architectures.

values.name: Non-LLM / classical agent core
values.reference: Russell & Norvig, AIMA — agent architectures (reflex, utility-based, learning agents); symbolic planners (PDDL/STRIPS), RL policies
values.justification: Historically the agent 'substrate' need not be an LLM at all; the field's broader taxonomy includes symbolic, planning, and RL policy cores, so the backbone extends beyond neural language models.

A.evidenceNeeded: A widely-adopted standard taxonomy that explicitly names "substrate" as an agent-configuration axis with a fixed value set (none exists today; model catalogs and serving-stack docs supply only an open, ever-growing list). Survey papers on agent architectures that formally separate the model axis from the runtime/serving axis would firm up whether the canonical backbone is provider-family, weights-openness, or serving-mode.

values.name: Frontier / proprietary API model (closed-weight, hosted)
values.reference: Stanford CRFM / HELM and the Foundation Model Transparency Index (Bommasani et al., 2023–2024); provider model cards (OpenAI GPT, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini)
values.justification: The dominant recognized substrate class for agents: a closed-weight foundation model accessed over a provider inference API — the canonical default backbone in production agent stacks.

values.name: Open-weight model (self-hostable foundation model)
values.reference: Llama (Meta, Touvron et al. 2023), Mistral/Mixtral, Qwen, DeepSeek; the 'open-weight' vs 'closed' distinction is standard in HELM / FMTI taxonomy
values.justification: Recognized field-standard counterpart to proprietary API models — weights are released, so the same agent can run on a fundamentally different (locally controllable) substrate.

values.name: Local / on-device runtime
values.reference: llama.cpp, Ollama, GGUF quantization ecosystem; MLC-LLM; the 'edge/on-device inference' category in systems-ML literature
values.justification: A distinct substrate class defined by where/how the model executes (consumer hardware, quantized, offline) rather than which model — a widely used backbone category.

values.name: Managed inference / serving runtime (cloud)
values.reference: vLLM (Kwon et al., SOSP 2023), TensorRT-LLM, Amazon Bedrock, Azure AI, Google Vertex, Together/Fireworks
values.justification: The serving-engine layer is a recognized substrate axis: the same weights run on different runtimes with different latency/throughput/cost characteristics.

values.name: Model size / capability tier
values.reference: Scaling-laws literature (Kaplan et al. 2020; Hoffmann/Chinchilla 2022); provider tiering (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku, GPT-4o/mini)
values.justification: A canonical sub-axis of substrate — agents are routinely configured by capability tier (large reasoning model vs small fast model), an established trade-off dimension.

values.name: Specific model ID / version (free-extension leaf)
values.reference: Provider model registries and Hugging Face Hub model identifiers (e.g., claude-opus, gpt-4o, llama-3.1-70b)
values.justification: Demonstrates the open tail: the concrete substrate value is an unbounded, continually-growing namespace of versioned model identifiers with no closed enum.

B.evidenceNeeded: A widely-adopted standards body taxonomy for 'agent substrate' (none currently exists comparable to SAE J3016 for autonomy). Confidence would rise with a cited canonical categorization of inference substrates from HELM/FMTI or an MLSys survey that explicitly enumerates substrate classes, vs. the current situation where the backbone categories (proprietary-API / open-weight / on-device / managed-serving / capability-tier) are conventional but the leaf (specific model versions) is provably open and unbounded.

values.name: Goal-based / utility-maximizing agent (the formal locus of telos)
values.reference: Russell & Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach — agent taxonomy (simple reflex / model-based / goal-based / utility-based / learning)
values.justification: AI's canonical statement that an agent has an ultimate end is the goal-based and utility-based agent; but the goal/utility CONTENT is application-supplied, which is exactly why telos is open at the content level.

values.name: Self-transcendence vs. self-enhancement / openness vs. conservation (value poles)
values.reference: Schwartz Theory of Basic Human Values (10 values on a circumplex: self-direction, stimulation, hedonism, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition, benevolence, universalism)
values.justification: The most empirically validated, cross-culturally replicated finite taxonomy of ultimate human motivational ends — a recognized backbone for what a human-aligned agent is 'driven toward'.

values.name: Archetypal core desire (e.g., Hero=mastery, Caregiver=service, Explorer=freedom, Sage=truth, Creator=creation, Ruler=control)
values.reference: Jungian archetype theory as operationalized by Mark & Pearson, The Hero and the Outlaw (12 brand archetypes, each defined by a single core desire/goal)
values.justification: A widely-used finite taxonomy in brand/persona design that maps one ultimate drive per archetype — directly a telos enumeration, but one competing lens among several.

values.name: Autonomy / competence / relatedness (intrinsic goal triad)
values.reference: Deci & Ryan, Self-Determination Theory
values.justification: Canonical psychology account of the basic intrinsic ends organisms are driven toward; offers a small finite backbone but is a different partition than Schwartz or archetypes.

values.name: Basic human needs as drivers (achievement, affiliation, power)
values.reference: McClelland, Human Motivation (acquired-needs theory); cf. Reiss 16 basic desires
values.justification: Another recognized finite enumeration of ultimate drives; its coexistence with SDT, Schwartz, and Reiss shows there is no single authoritative enum — hence hybrid, not closed.

values.name: Application-specified objective (free extension)
values.reference: AI agent practice — objective functions / mission statements / system-prompt 'your purpose is…' (no standard taxonomy)
values.justification: In deployed agents the telos is most often a bespoke, free-form objective (e.g., 'maximize customer resolution', 'minimize latency'), demonstrating the open tail beyond any psychological backbone.

A.evidenceNeeded: Evidence that any ONE taxonomy is treated as authoritative for AGENT telos specifically (not human motivation by analogy) would shift this toward closed; conversely, a survey of agent system-prompt 'purpose' fields showing no convergence would confirm the open tail. Key uncertainty: whether the field wants telos as a content enum at all, or only as the abstract structural property (goal-/utility-based agent) with content left free — the latter favors a cleaner 'open' classification with the psychological taxonomies as optional scaffolds.

values.name: The Hero (drive: mastery / prove worth through courageous action)
values.reference: Jungian brand archetypes — Mark & Pearson, The Hero and the Outlaw (2001); the 12-archetype system
values.justification: In the most widely-used finite taxonomy of motivational identity, the Hero is the canonical archetype whose defining telos is mastery and proving worth — a recognized member of a closed 12-set.

values.name: The Caregiver (drive: protect and care for others)
values.reference: Jungian brand archetypes — Mark & Pearson (2001), 12-archetype model
values.justification: Canonical archetype whose ultimate purpose is altruistic protection; one of the four 'belonging/service' archetypes in the standard wheel.

values.name: The Sage / Explorer (drive: understand the world / seek truth and freedom)
values.reference: Jungian brand archetypes — Mark & Pearson (2001)
values.justification: The Sage (truth, knowledge) and Explorer (freedom, discovery) are canonical members capturing the epistemic/autonomy telos most relevant to assistant agents.

values.name: Autonomy / Competence / Relatedness (the three intrinsic ends)
values.reference: Self-Determination Theory — Deci & Ryan (1985, 2000)
values.justification: SDT names a small, recognized backbone of intrinsic psychological needs that function as ultimate motivational ends — a finite, empirically grounded telos set.

values.name: Basic desires (e.g. Power, Curiosity, Order, Acceptance, Idealism)
values.reference: Reiss's 16 Basic Desires — Steven Reiss (Who Am I?, 2000)
values.justification: An empirically factor-derived finite taxonomy of intrinsic human motivators, each an 'ultimate end pursued for its own sake' — directly a closed enumeration of teloi.

values.name: Free-form goal / utility function (open extension)
values.reference: AI agent architecture — Russell & Norvig (AIMA): goal-based and utility-based agents; BDI (Rao & Georgeff, 1995)
values.justification: In the agent-engineering literature itself, telos is the agent's desire set / performance measure — arbitrary content, not drawn from any enum; this is the open arm that makes the dimension hybrid rather than closed.

B.evidenceNeeded: Whether the cataloging effort intends 'telos' as (a) a motivational-identity slot, in which case the Mark & Pearson 12-archetype wheel is the strongest closed backbone, or (b) a literal goal/objective slot, in which case AIMA/BDI treat it as fully open. Confirmation of which discipline is authoritative for this organ, plus whether any single framework (archetypes vs. SDT vs. Reiss) is being adopted as the canonical backbone, would sharpen the closed/hybrid call and let the value list collapse to one provenance.
